Any consistent system rich enough to describe arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove from within its own axioms, and the system cannot prove its own consistency either. The result did not stop mathematicians working, but it closed off Hilbert's programme for good and reshaped what a proof could be asked to guarantee.

After his mother Helena travelled to Jerusalem, Constantine ordered a temple to Jupiter, or in some accounts to Venus, torn down on a site local Christians had long identified as Golgotha. Workers digging beneath it uncovered a rock-cut tomb that Bishop Eusebius, writing at the time, described as the burial place venerated as Christ's.

Constantine had the surrounding rock cut away to leave the tomb standing free, and built the Church of the Holy Sepulchre around it, completed around 335 CE. Almost nothing of that first Constantinian church survives after later destructions and rebuildings, but the site itself has been continuously venerated and fought over ever since.

Google Earth grew out of a program called EarthViewer 3D, built by a company called Keyhole that Google bought in 2004. The software stitched together satellite photographs and aerial imagery over a rotating three-dimensional globe, and Google released it free to the public in June 2005, letting anyone zoom from orbit down to street-level rooftops.

The tool had been built for intelligence and defence work, and its name nodded to the Keyhole spy satellite program, but the free release opened the same imagery to journalists tracking troop movements, archaeologists spotting buried structures from above, and ordinary users looking up their own house for the first time from space.

Gorm is the earliest Danish king named in a source contemporary with his own reign rather than written generations later, which is why historians treat him, ruling from around 936, as the first Danish monarch who can be placed with any confidence rather than a legendary figure.

He ruled from Jelling in Jutland, where he raised a burial mound and the older of the two Jelling runestones, carved by his son Harald Bluetooth in his memory. The present Danish monarchy still traces its line back to Gorm without a break, which makes it, by that reckoning, the oldest continuous monarchy in Europe.

The United States Air Force declared the Global Positioning System fully operational on 17 July 1995, once 24 satellites were in place across six orbital planes, enough for a receiver anywhere on the ground to see at least four at once at all times. Earlier satellites had already let the system work intermittently since the late 1980s, but full coverage removed the gaps.

The constellation had been built chiefly for military navigation and precision weapons targeting, and civilian receivers were deliberately fed a degraded signal under a policy called Selective Availability. That restriction was switched off in 2000 on presidential order, sharpening civilian accuracy from roughly 100 metres to about 10, and opening the door to the everyday car and phone navigation that followed.

Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, working at the University of Manchester, used ordinary sticky tape to peel flakes off a block of graphite, the material in a pencil, then pressed the tape together and pulled it apart repeatedly to thin the flakes further. Some ended up only one atom thick, a sheet of carbon arranged in a honeycomb lattice that nobody had isolated and tested before.

Graphene turned out to conduct electricity better than copper, hold more strength for its weight than steel, and remain flexible, properties that had mostly been predicted on paper. The two shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics, and the tape-and-graphite method, dubbed exfoliation, is still taught as an entry point into two-dimensional materials research.

Antoine Rossignol and his son Bonaventure built their cipher for Louis XIV's most sensitive correspondence around 1650, using numbers to stand for whole French syllables rather than single letters, with some numbers assigned to cancel the syllable before them. That trick alone defeated the usual frequency-counting attacks that broke ordinary substitution ciphers of the age.

When the Rossignols died, nobody who knew the system remained, and encoded despatches sat unread in French archives for two centuries. Army cryptographer Etienne Bazeries spent three years on it and cracked the syllable structure around 1893, finally reading letters that included the identity of a long-rumoured masked prisoner, the Man in the Iron Mask.

The clock above the new Palace of Westminster, rebuilt after the 1834 fire that destroyed most of the old Houses of Parliament, was designed to unusually strict standards: lawyer and clockmaker Edmund Beckett Denison insisted it strike the first stroke of each hour accurate to within a second. Astronomer Royal George Airy backed the demand, and it took engineer Edward Dent years to build a mechanism that could meet it.

The clock began keeping time in 1859, and its bell, cast at the Whitechapel Bell Foundry and officially named the Great Bell, quickly picked up the nickname Big Ben, later applied loosely to the whole tower. The tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower only in 2012, for the queen's diamond jubilee.

By the mid 1540s Henry VIII had spent through the wealth seized from the monasteries and was still fighting wars in France and Scotland. The mints began replacing silver in the coinage with copper, dropping the fineness of the shilling from around 92 per cent silver toward a fraction of that, while keeping the coin's face value and stamped weight unchanged.

Silver-plated copper wore through fastest at the king's own nose on the coin's profile, earning Henry the nickname Old Coppernose. Prices rose sharply as merchants adjusted for the debased metal, and the mess took until 1560, under Elizabeth I, to unwind through a formal recoinage that withdrew the bad silver from circulation.

France adopted the Great Paris Cipher at the end of 1811, a table of roughly 1,400 numbers standing for letters, syllables and whole words, meant to defeat exactly the kind of interception Wellington relied on. Major George Scovell built up a stack of captured despatches through 1812, using the fragments of plain French that crept into supposedly coded letters to work back toward the substitutions.

The breakthrough came in December 1812, when Scovell decrypted a letter from Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon's brother and the nominal king of Spain, that laid out French troop movements in enough detail to shape Wellington's own planning. Scovell kept working the cipher through the war's final campaigns, and his notebooks survive in the National Archives.

William Lambton began the survey in 1802 under the East India Company, dragging a half-ton theodolite across southern India to chain a continuous line of triangles from Cape Comorin northward. He called the project the Great Indian Arc of the Meridian, aiming simply to fix the exact curvature of the Earth along one long north-south line.

The survey outlived Lambton, who died in the field in 1823, and ran under his successor George Everest for decades more before reaching the Himalayan foothills around 1841. It was there that surveyors, working from triangulated distances rather than direct measurement, calculated the height of a peak later named Everest after him, though he himself never saw it.

At a Greek symposium, wine was never drunk neat. It was mixed with water in a large krater, typically at ratios weighted toward water, and ladled out to guests reclining on couches, since drinking wine unmixed was considered a habit of barbarians rather than civilised men.

A symposiarch set the mixing ratio and paced the evening's toasts, while poetry, riddles and music filled the gaps between rounds of drinking. The practice, attested from around 600 BCE onward in Greek pottery and poetry, treated drunkenness as something to be managed by convention rather than avoided outright.

The Julian calendar overcounted the year by about 11 minutes, which by 1582 had pushed the spring equinox ten days out of line with the calendar date used to fix Easter. Pope Gregory XIII's bull Inter Gravissimas ordered ten days struck from October that year, so 4 October was followed directly by 15 October in the countries that adopted it immediately.

The reform also changed which century years count as leap years, dropping three leap days every four centuries so the calendar and the solar year would stay aligned far longer. Catholic states adopted it at once, but Protestant and Orthodox states held out for generations. Britain and its colonies did not switch until 1752, and Russia waited until 1918.

William Grey Walter was a neurologist at the Burden Neurological Institute in Bristol, studying brainwaves with EEG machines, when he built two small three-wheeled robots between 1948 and 1949 to test how few components could produce lifelike behaviour. He named them Elmer and Elsie, acronyms built loosely around electro-mechanical robot and light sensitivity.

Each had a single photocell and a touch sensor wired to two motors, giving it just two working nerve cells, yet the tortoises wandered rooms, steered toward dim light while avoiding glare, and nosed their way back to a hutch to recharge when their batteries ran low. Walter used them to argue that complex behaviour did not require a complex nervous system, an early and influential claim of the new field of cybernetics.

Arthur Guinness took over the disused St James's Gate brewery in Dublin on 31 December 1759 on a lease running nine thousand years at an annual rent of 45 pounds, terms generous enough that the brewery still occupies the site under a version of that same agreement today, long after the figure became a marketing story in its own right.

Guinness brewed ale at first and only later switched the site over to the dark porter that made the name famous, a style he had already brewed elsewhere in Dublin. The nine thousand years have outlasted the Georgian city around the gate, several changes of Irish government and the brewery's own growth into a multinational company.

Divers off Bahrain and the wider Persian Gulf worked oyster beds on a single held breath, weighted by a stone tied to one foot and guided down by a rope, surfacing after roughly a minute with a net of shells. Assyrian and Indian traders bought the pearls, a trade attested by the eighth century BCE and likely older still.

The diving season ran through the hot summer months, and divers worked in teams from small boats, splitting the season's haul with the boat's owner under customary shares that persisted into the twentieth century. Cultured pearls from Japan collapsed this economy in the 1930s, ending a livelihood the Gulf had kept for centuries.

Gustav Vasa had spent the previous years leading a rebellion against Danish rule that began among the miners and farmers of Dalarna, after Christian II of Denmark executed dozens of Swedish nobles and clergy in the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520. By the time he was elected king at Strangnas on 6 June 1523, Stockholm itself was about to fall to his forces.

His election ended the Kalmar Union, which had bound Sweden, Denmark and Norway under one crown since 1397, and Denmark formally recognised Swedish independence within weeks. Gustav went on to break the church's landholdings and pass the crown to his own descendants, turning a wartime election into the founding reign of an independent Swedish state.

At the 1996 International AIDS Conference in Vancouver, researchers including David Ho presented results showing that combining a protease inhibitor with two older antiretroviral drugs could drive HIV to undetectable levels in the blood. Any one of the drugs alone let the virus mutate around it within weeks; three together closed off that escape route.

Death rates from AIDS in the United States fell sharply within a couple of years of the therapy reaching clinics, and obituary pages that had listed young men by the column shrank. The drugs were expensive and demanding, dozens of pills on a strict schedule, and for years reached wealthy countries long before they reached the parts of Africa where the epidemic was worst.

John Scott Haldane approached diving sickness as a plumbing problem rather than a mysterious ailment. Divers surfacing quickly from depth were falling ill and sometimes dying because nitrogen, dissolved in their blood under pressure, formed bubbles as that pressure dropped, and his 1908 study set out to work out how slowly a diver had to rise to let the gas leave the body without bubbling.

Haldane's tables, produced with the Royal Navy, prescribed a series of stops at set depths on the way up rather than a single steady ascent, giving tissues time to release nitrogen gradually. Staged decompression, refined many times since, remains the basic method divers use to avoid decompression sickness, still generally known by its old nickname, the bends.

Edmond Halley is remembered for the comet, but in 1690 he was also building diving equipment, an open-bottomed bell weighted with lead and supplied by a second, smaller weighted barrel lowered from the surface. Water pressure forced fresh air from the barrel up into the bell as it was drawn level with the opening, letting a diver breathe without ever surfacing.

In a demonstration in the Thames, Halley and several companions sat inside the bell at a depth of about 60 feet for over an hour and a half, and he later extended dives to more than four hours with refinements. The bell proved too heavy and cumbersome for real salvage work, but it showed that a supplied air pocket, rather than held breath, was the way to keep divers down.

William Rowan Hamilton had spent years trying to extend complex numbers into three dimensions, to describe rotations in space with a single algebra, and kept failing because a three-term system would not multiply consistently. Walking with his wife along the Royal Canal in Dublin on 16 October 1843, he suddenly saw that four terms, not three, would work if he let multiplication stop being commutative.

Unable to find paper, he carved the founding formula, i squared equals j squared equals k squared equals ijk equals minus one, into the stone of Broom Bridge. A plaque there still marks the spot. Quaternions never replaced ordinary vectors for most physics, but they survive today inside the software that rotates objects in video games and spacecraft without the errors ordinary rotation matrices accumulate.

The rule usually retold as a ban on watering down beer is something narrower. Law 108 of Hammurabi's code, cut into diorite around 1750 BCE, targeted tavern keepers who took payment in silver rather than grain and shortchanged the customer on the price. Beer was rationed and traded in fixed grain measures, so a mismatch was easy to prove, and the law punished it by drowning.

Other clauses in the same code fixed how much beer a labourer, a temple worker or a child was owed as a ration, because beer was a barley staple rather than a luxury. The keepers named in these laws were usually women, running the alehouses that were Babylon's ordinary drinking houses, open to the same scrutiny as any bread or grain seller.

In a 1974 paper in Nature, Stephen Hawking argued that black holes should not be perfect traps at all. Applying quantum theory to the region just outside the event horizon, he found that pairs of particles constantly flicker into existence there, and occasionally one escapes while its partner falls in, carrying mass away from the hole as it goes.

The consequence unsettled physicists more than the mechanism did: a black hole radiating energy must slowly lose mass and, given enough time, evaporate completely. No instrument has yet detected the effect directly, since the radiation from any real astrophysical black hole would be far fainter than the cosmic background around it, but the prediction reshaped how physicists think about gravity and information.

Helike was a leading city of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth, prosperous enough to have founded colonies in Italy, when an earthquake and a wave from the sea struck it in the winter of 373 BC. Ancient writers say the destruction was total and that every inhabitant died, with only fragments of buildings left showing above the waterline.

For centuries the site was known only from those accounts, visible as ruins under shallow water that later silted over and vanished. A Greek-American survey team located the buried city on the coastal plain in 2001, using sonar and drilling rather than diving, and continuing excavation has since raised a competing theory that the flooding came from landward drainage rather than a tsunami alone.

Peter Henlein was a Nuremberg locksmith, not a member of any watchmakers' guild, since no such guild yet existed for the trade he was effectively inventing. Around 1510 he was building small spring driven clocks, wound rather than weight driven, compact enough to be carried on the body rather than mounted on a wall or tower, work that later writers credited as the origin of the pocket watch.

Henlein's fame as the sole inventor rests heavily on a nineteenth century German novel that turned him into a folk hero long after his death in 1542, and other German clockmakers of the same period were producing similarly small spring driven timepieces. No verified example signed by Henlein survives, so his exact contribution is harder to pin down than the legend built around his name.

Henry was hunting in the New Forest when word reached him that his brother William II had died there, shot by an arrow whose origin was never satisfactorily explained. Henry rode straight for Westminster and was crowned within days, before his elder brother Robert, away on crusade, could contest the throne.

To buy the barons' support for a rushed and shaky claim, Henry issued a coronation charter promising to end the abuses of William's reign: arbitrary seizure of church property, forced marriages of heiresses, extortionate fines. Copies were sent to cathedrals across England, and one surfaced again over a century later as a template the barons handed to King John at Runnymede.

Nineteen years of civil war between Stephen and the Empress Matilda, later called the Anarchy, had left England's crown lands plundered and its baronage used to fighting each other. The 1153 Treaty of Wallingford let Stephen keep the throne for his lifetime on condition that Matilda's son Henry succeed him, and Stephen died the following October.

Henry was crowned in December 1154 already ruling Normandy, Anjou and, through his wife Eleanor of Aquitaine, territory stretching to the Pyrenees, an assemblage historians later called the Angevin Empire. He spent much of his 34 year reign rebuilding royal authority the Anarchy had let slip, reforming the courts and reasserting control over barons grown used to acting on their own.

Henry IV had ended decades of civil war between Catholics and Huguenots with the Edict of Nantes in 1598, granting Protestants legal toleration, though he himself had converted to Catholicism to secure the throne. On 14 May 1610, his carriage was stopped in a narrow Paris street by traffic, and Francois Ravaillac climbed onto a wheel and stabbed him.

Ravaillac, a fervent Catholic who believed the king was about to make war on the Pope, was captured on the spot and executed within days by public torture and dismemberment. Henry's death left the throne to his nine year old son, Louis XIII, under his mother Marie de Medici's regency, and reopened the political instability his reign had spent years closing down.

Henry VI was not yet ten years old when Notre-Dame Cathedral hosted his coronation as French king, on 16 December 1431, nine years after infancy had already made him King of England. English forces had held Paris since 1420 under the Treaty of Troyes, which disinherited the French dauphin, and the Paris ceremony was staged to make that claim visible to a population never fully persuaded by it.

By then Joan of Arc had already forced Charles VII's rival coronation at Reims two years earlier, and English fortunes in France were already turning. Henry remains the only English monarch ever crowned king of France, a title the English crown kept claiming on paper for centuries after the country itself was lost.

A well-digger near modern Resina, working in 1709 for a French prince building a villa above, struck marble far underground rather than the water he was after. The marble turned out to be seating from a Roman theatre buried under roughly twenty metres of hardened volcanic material, laid down when Vesuvius destroyed Herculaneum alongside Pompeii in 79 CE.

Early recovery was closer to looting than excavation: statues and inscribed marble were hauled up through shafts and tunnels dug straight into the rock, with little record kept of where anything had actually stood. Organised digging did not begin for decades, but the well is generally treated as the moment Herculaneum's existence, buried and largely forgotten, became known again.

Drawn on a single calfskin around 1300 and still hanging in Hereford Cathedral, this map is the largest medieval world map to survive intact. It puts Jerusalem at the centre of a circular world with east, not north, at the top, because the map orders the world through Christian history rather than through direction a traveller could use.

Around its edges are Biblical scenes, mythical peoples, and creatures like the manticore and the phoenix jostling with real cities and rivers, none drawn to a scale that would help anyone find their way. It functioned less as a navigational tool than as a visual encyclopaedia of everything believed about the world, compressed onto roughly five feet of stretched hide.

William Herschel, who had discovered Uranus four years earlier, spent the mid-1780s pointing his own hand-built telescopes at hundreds of patches of sky and simply counting the stars visible in each, on the assumption that stars thinned out evenly toward the galaxy's edge and that their density told him its shape.

From those counts he published a diagram in 1785 showing the Milky Way as a flattened, irregular disc with the sun somewhere near its middle, the first attempt to chart the galaxy's structure from direct observation rather than speculation. The method's assumptions were flawed, since interstellar dust hid distant stars and skewed the counts, but the basic disc shape held up.

Judean workers cut the roughly 530-metre Siloam Tunnel through solid limestone beneath Jerusalem around 700 BCE, working from the Gihon Spring at one end and the Pool of Siloam at the other. An inscription found inside, now in Istanbul, describes the moment the two crews heard each other's picks and broke through.

The tunnel's winding, S-shaped course has puzzled engineers, since a straight line would have been shorter; one theory is that the diggers followed a natural crack in the rock rather than a surveyed line. It gave Jerusalem a hidden water supply during Sennacherib's siege, when the Assyrian king cut off the spring outside the walls.

Muslim administrators around 638 needed to date letters and contracts, and the caliph Umar had to pick a starting point. He rejected Muhammad's birth and settled on the migration, the hijra, from Mecca to Medina in 622, fixing that year as year one of a lunar calendar of twelve months with no leap month to keep it aligned to the sun.

Because the lunar year runs about eleven days shorter than the solar year, Islamic dates drift steadily against the seasons rather than repeating on fixed solar dates, which is why Ramadan falls in a different season each decade. The Hijri calendar remains the official calendar of Saudi Arabia and is used alongside civil calendars across the Muslim world.

David Hilbert had prepared far more than he delivered. His lecture to the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris in 1900 covered only about ten of the problems he had drafted; the full list of twenty-three was printed afterwards, and it is the printed list, not the speech, that mathematicians have chased ever since.

The problems ranged from Cantor's continuum hypothesis to the consistency of arithmetic itself, and Hilbert framed them less as a checklist than as a bet on where the field's effort would pay off. Some were settled within years, some took most of a century, and one, the Riemann hypothesis, is still open, still treated as one of mathematics' hardest unsolved questions.

Hipparchus worked from Rhodes with a catalogue of star positions and a set of Babylonian eclipse records already centuries old by his time. Checking his own measurements against them, he found that the equinox point had shifted against the fixed stars, a drift too small to see in one lifetime but unmistakable across generations of records.

He put the shift at roughly one degree per century, close to the modern figure of about one degree every seventy two years. The effect, precession of the equinoxes, comes from the Earth's axis slowly tracing a circle rather than pointing at one fixed spot in the sky, something no observer in the second century BCE could have known the cause of.

Histiaeus, tyrant of Miletus, was held as a guest-prisoner at the Persian court in Susa when he decided to incite revolt back home. According to Herodotus, he had a trusted slave's head shaved, tattooed a message onto the scalp, and waited for the hair to regrow before sending the man to Miletus around 499 BCE.

The recipient, Aristagoras, was told only to shave the messenger's head and read what was written there: an instruction to revolt against Persian rule. Whether or not the story is literally true, the revolt it triggered spread across Ionia and drew Athens into the fight, a chain of events that helped provoke the Persian invasions of Greece.

George V had ruled since 1910 as a member of the House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, a name that had suited nobody's mood by 1917, with Britain three years into a war against Germany and Zeppelins bombing London. On 17 July he issued a proclamation dropping every German title held by his family and adopting Windsor, after the castle, instead.

Cousins and in-laws followed suit: the Battenbergs became Mountbattens and other relatives took plain English surnames. The change was cosmetic in the sense that the bloodline did not alter, but it answered a real political problem, a monarchy whose family tree read as enemy aristocracy to a public burying its dead.

The H. L. Hunley was a cramped iron tube barely wide enough for its crew, propelled by eight men turning a hand crank connected to the propeller shaft, and it had already killed two previous crews, including its own inventor, in accidental sinkings during testing in Charleston harbour. On the night of 17 February 1864 it went out anyway, commanded by a fresh volunteer crew, to attack the Union blockade.

It rammed a spar tipped with a black powder charge into the hull of the USS Housatonic, sinking the sloop in minutes and killing five of her crew, the first warship ever destroyed by a submarine in combat. The Hunley itself vanished that same night with all eight men aboard, and its wreck was not located until 1995, still lying near the site of the attack.

A team aboard the research vessel Knorr set out in February 1977 to study the Galapagos Rift, roughly 400 miles west of Ecuador, expecting only to measure heat escaping through the seafloor. Within days of arriving, scientists riding in the submersible Alvin spotted a shimmering plume of hot water rising from cracks in the rock, and around it something nobody had predicted: dense clusters of life.

Foot-long white clams and thickets of tube worms crowded the vents in total darkness, thousands of metres below any sunlight. The find overturned an assumption that all life ultimately depends on photosynthesis, since these communities instead feed on bacteria that convert chemicals from the vent water into food. More than 500 vent fields have since been catalogued around the world's ocean ridges.

In March 415 a mob of Christian monks and their allies dragged Hypatia from her carriage in Alexandria, stripped her, and killed her inside a church. The killing followed a bitter feud between the city's prefect, Orestes, whom Hypatia advised, and Cyril, the bishop of Alexandria, over who held real authority in the city.

She had taught mathematics and Neoplatonist philosophy in Alexandria for decades, drawing pupils regardless of their faith. Almost none of her own writing survives; what is known of her work comes mostly through letters from her student Synesius and later Christian and pagan historians, whose accounts of her death do not fully agree on the details.

Ibn al-Haytham's Doubts Concerning Ptolemy, written around 1028, did not offer a replacement cosmos. It laid out, point by point, where Ptolemy's own geometry contradicted itself: the equant point that let planets move at uneven speed around no physical centre, a device Ptolemy needed to match observation but could not explain mechanically.

Ibn al-Haytham insisted that a true model of the heavens had to correspond to real physical bodies moving uniformly, not just save appearances on paper. That demand shaped astronomers across the Islamic world for two centuries afterward, and historians now trace a line from his objections through later reworkings of planetary theory toward the eventual break with an Earth centred sky.

Ibn al-Shatir worked in Damascus as the muwaqqit, the mosque official responsible for timing the call to prayer by astronomical calculation, a job that demanded models accurate enough for practical use rather than philosophical elegance. Around 1350 he produced a full planetary theory that discarded Ptolemy's equant, using instead combinations of uniformly rotating circles in the tradition developed at the Maragha observatory.

His lunar model in particular corrected a long standing flaw in Ptolemy's, which made the Moon's apparent size vary far more than observation showed. The geometry Ibn al-Shatir used to fix it reappears, essentially unchanged, in Copernicus's own lunar theory two centuries later, though no direct transmission route between the two has ever been proven.

Ibn Sahl worked at the Abbasid court in Baghdad on a treatise called On Burning Mirrors and Lenses, finished around 984. To design lenses that focus light without distortion, he needed to know exactly how a ray bends when it passes from air into glass, and he worked out the constant ratio that governs it.

That ratio is what later became known in Europe as Snell's law, after the Dutch astronomer who reached it independently more than six centuries afterward. Ibn Sahl's manuscript, rediscovered in a Damascus library only in the twentieth century, shows the same geometry drawn out with a straightedge and compass, six hundred years earlier.

Denmark could not object. Nazi Germany had occupied it since 1940, and Iceland, garrisoned instead by British and American troops, held a referendum in May 1944 in which nearly every voter backed severing the centuries-old link to the Danish crown. The break was less a rupture than a formality nobody in Copenhagen was in a position to contest.

On 17 June 1944, the birthday of the independence campaigner Jon Sigurdsson, delegates gathered in the rain at Thingvellir, the site of Iceland's medieval assembly, to proclaim the republic and swear in Sveinn Bjornsson as its first president. The date has been Iceland's national day ever since, tying the new republic to a parliament nearly a thousand years older than it.

Australia's environment minister, Malcolm Turnbull, announced in February 2007 that the country would stop selling incandescent filament bulbs by 2010, framing it as an easy way to cut household electricity use and greenhouse emissions since the bulbs waste most of their power as heat rather than light.

The idea spread fast: the European Union adopted a similar phase-out later that year, and the United States followed with efficiency standards in its 2007 energy bill that effectively ended the century-old bulb by the mid-2010s. Compact fluorescents and then LED bulbs took its place, using a fraction of the electricity for the same brightness.

No text from the discovery survives, and even the name attached to it is uncertain. Later Greek writers credit a Pythagorean, sometimes named as Hippasus, with the proof around the mid fifth century BC, though the school itself is said to have treated the finding as unwelcome rather than triumphant.

The proof works by contradiction: assume the diagonal of a unit square can be written as a fraction in lowest terms, and the arithmetic forces both its numerator and denominator to be even, which lowest terms forbids. That broke the Pythagorean belief that all quantities reduce to whole-number ratios, and later legend punished the discovery with the messenger's drowning.

Richard Lawrence, an unemployed house painter who believed himself a deposed king owed money by the United States government, stepped out as Andrew Jackson left a congressional funeral in the Capitol on 30 January 1835. His first pistol misfired at close range; he cocked a second and it misfired too, both later found properly loaded and in working order.

Jackson, sixty-seven, went after Lawrence with his cane before bystanders, including Congressman Davy Crockett, pulled the men apart. Lawrence was tried and found not guilty by reason of insanity, spending the rest of his life in asylums, and the episode remains the first assassination attempt on a sitting American president.

Smallpox reached Japan through the port province of Kyushu around 735, most likely carried by a diplomatic mission returning from Tang China or the Korean peninsula, and spread north through a population with no prior immunity. Records from the imperial court describe entire households dying and fields left unharvested as the epidemic ran through 737.

Modern estimates, drawn from tax and census records of the time, put the death toll at roughly a quarter to a third of Japan's population, including several of the era's most powerful courtiers, the Fujiwara brothers who had dominated the government. Emperor Shomu responded by commissioning Buddhist temples and a great bronze statue at Nara, seeking protection the court could not otherwise provide.

Before the andon, Japanese households lit rooms with open oil dishes or torches that smoked and guttered in draughts. The andon enclosed a small wick floating in rapeseed oil inside a wooden frame covered with washi paper, which spread the flame's light evenly across a room while shielding it from wind, making it safer to leave burning through the night.

By the mid sixteenth century the andon had become the standard household lamp across Japan, portable versions carried by a handle and fixed ones left by a doorway or bedside. Its paper panels also made it a natural surface for painted decoration, and the same basic frame, wick and oil design stayed in ordinary use for roughly three centuries until kerosene and, later, electric light replaced it.

Pierre Jaquet-Droz and his son built three automata in Neuchatel through the 1770s to advertise the family's watchmaking: a musician who played a real organ, a draughtsman who sketched, and the Writer, a seated boy who dipped a quill in ink, shook off the excess and wrote out a text letter by letter.

The words were not fixed. A disc of interchangeable cams inside the boy's body could be swapped to write up to forty characters chosen by the operator, making it programmable in a real if limited sense, decades before the word existed. All three automata survive and still run at a museum in Neuchatel, wound up for demonstration a few times a year.

Jefferson's design used thirty-six wheels rather than the twenty-six later popularised, each with a scrambled alphabet on its rim, threaded on a single spindle so the whole assembly could be twisted to spell a plaintext along one row and read the cipher off any other. No two wheels carried the letters in the same order, which meant the key was the sequence the wheels sat in, not a code word.

He drew it up around 1795 while serving as secretary of state but never had it built or adopted, and the design sat unpublished among his papers. The United States Army independently reinvented the same wheel arrangement in the early twentieth century and used it as the M-94 cipher device, unaware Jefferson had already worked it out over a century earlier.

The Schlick family had been minting silver on their own authority at Joachimsthal, in the Bohemian mountains, before the crown noticed. Official approval came on 1 January 1520, and on 9 January the mint began striking large coins of roughly 27.6 grams, close to 93 per cent pure, stamped with Saint Joachim on one face and the Bohemian lion on the other.

The coin was named for the valley, Joachimsthal, and shortened across German-speaking Europe to thaler. Dutch and Scandinavian variants followed the same silver standard, and English merchants trading with the Low Countries picked up the word as daler, which became dollar. A mining town's local currency ended up naming the money of nations it never traded with directly.

Warren Johnson taught at a Wisconsin normal school and grew tired of janitors misjudging classroom temperature by hand, running boilers too hot or too cold before anyone noticed. His 1883 patent used a bimetallic strip that bent as the room's air warmed or cooled, and that small bend closed an electric circuit which signalled a damper to open or shut.

The invention did not stay a schoolroom fix. Johnson founded a company to build and sell his thermostats commercially, and the firm grew into a major supplier of building controls. The basic idea, a physical change in a sensor triggering a remote mechanical response, remained the working principle behind home thermostats for the next century.

Rome's old calendar tracked the moon and relied on priests to insert extra months to keep it aligned with the seasons, a job they had neglected or manipulated for political reasons until the calendar had drifted roughly two to three months out of step with the sun. Caesar, advised by the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes, fixed the year at 365 days with a leap day every fourth year.

To bring the calendar back into line at all, 46 BCE itself ran to 445 days, absorbing the accumulated slippage in one stretch later Romans called the year of confusion. The Julian calendar then held, essentially unchanged, until Pope Gregory XIII corrected its slight overcount of leap years in 1582.

Justinian's sixth century compilation of Roman legal opinions, the Digest, had all but vanished from use in the West for five hundred years, surviving mainly in a single manuscript, the Littera Florentina. Its reappearance in northern Italy around 1070 gave scholars a complete, organised body of Roman civil law where before there had been only fragments and custom.

At Bologna, teachers built a formal school of law around close reading of the Digest, glossing its text line by line for students drawn from across Europe. That method, and the graduates it produced, spread Roman legal concepts into the courts and universities of the continent long before any single state adopted the code wholesale.

Chinese cities had long enforced a curfew that shut markets and closed gates at dusk, a rule going back to Tang law codes meant to keep order after dark. By the early twelfth century, Kaifeng, the Song capital, was letting stalls stay open under lamplight well past that hour, selling cooked food, wine and small goods to a population the old curfew could no longer contain.

A famous scroll and contemporary accounts describe streets still busy at what earlier dynasties would have called the dead of night, with vendors trading until the small hours. The change reflected a capital that had simply outgrown the old rhythm of an agrarian city, and it fed a wider Song era shift toward a cash economy running on something closer to a modern clock.

The Japanese remotely operated vehicle Kaiko descended into the Challenger Deep, the lowest point of the Mariana Trench, on 24 March 1995, recording a depth of about 10,911 metres. It was only the second craft ever to reach that spot on the seafloor, after the crewed submersible Trieste's dive in 1960, and the first to return there in the 35 years between.

Because Kaiko carried no crew, operators on the surface ship could keep it down far longer than a manned submersible and send it back repeatedly without risking anyone's life. On later dives it recovered mud cores and small crustaceans called amphipods living at crushing pressure in total darkness. Kaiko itself was lost at sea in 2003 after a typhoon severed its control cable.

Vatsyayana's Kama Sutra is remembered outside India almost entirely for its chapters on sex, but most of the text is a manual of behaviour for an educated household, running through hospitality, courtship, and a list of sixty four arts a cultured man or woman was expected to know. Cooking, music, and gambling all appear on that list.

One entry, mlecchita vikalpa, covers techniques for writing in cipher, useful for lovers exchanging letters that a household could not read if intercepted. Later commentators described specific methods, including swapping letters in matched pairs, though the text itself gives little technical detail, treating cryptography as one social skill among many rather than a subject in its own right.

The Kangnido, drawn in Korea in 1402 under the Joseon official Kwon Kun, places China at an enormous, dominating centre and shrinks Korea and Japan around its edges, a choice of scale that reflects diplomacy rather than geography. It drew on two Chinese maps brought back by envoys, one of which already incorporated Islamic geographic data, so an outline of Africa and a recognisable Iberian peninsula appear on it decades before direct contact.

No original survives. What exists are Japanese copies from the 1470s onward, kept at Buddhist temples, through which the map reached the modern world at all. It is one of the earliest surviving maps to show Africa's true southward shape rather than a vague fringe, made decades before any European voyage credited with charting that coast.

In 1755, the philosopher Immanuel Kant, then an obscure lecturer at Konigsberg, published a cosmology essay proposing that the faint, cloud-like nebulae astronomers catalogued were not gas within our own star system but entire galaxies of stars, comparable to the Milky Way and scattered through space at vast distances from it.

He had no telescope capable of resolving one and offered the idea as reasoned speculation rather than observation. It took until the 1920s, when Edwin Hubble measured the distance to the Andromeda nebula and showed it lay far beyond the Milky Way, for Kant's guess to be confirmed as fact rather than philosophy.

The Vigenere cipher, which shifted each letter of a message by a different amount according to a repeating keyword, had been called le chiffre indechiffrable for three centuries because no general method existed to break it without already knowing the key. A cryptanalyst facing an unknown keyword length was, in practice, stuck.

Friedrich Kasiski, a retired Prussian infantry officer, published a solution in 1863: search the ciphertext for repeated letter sequences, since a repeated plaintext word encrypted at the same point in the keyword's cycle produces a repeated fragment, and the distances between those repeats reveal the key's length as a common factor. Charles Babbage found the same method earlier but never published it.

Chemists in the 1860s knew benzene's formula, six carbon atoms and six hydrogen, but could not draw a structure that fit the usual rules of carbon bonding without leaving something unexplained. August Kekule later described dozing by a fire in 1865 and seeing a vision of atoms as a snake twisting and then seizing its own tail, which gave him the idea of a closed ring rather than an open chain.

A hexagonal ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen, explained benzene's properties neatly and became the foundation of aromatic chemistry, the study of ring compounds that behave unlike ordinary chains. Kekule told the snake story decades after the fact, at a chemists' gathering, and historians still debate how literally to take it, but the ring structure itself was quickly confirmed and never seriously challenged.

Auguste Kerckhoffs was a Dutch linguist teaching in France, not a soldier, when he published La Cryptographie Militaire in 1883. His central claim ran against the instinct of every army that had ever tried to hide how its ciphers worked: a system that only stays safe while its method is secret is not actually safe, because methods leak, get captured, or get guessed.

Kerckhoffs set out several requirements for a workable military cipher, but the one that survived is that everything about the system except the key should be assumed known to the enemy. Modern cryptography still designs to that standard: publish the algorithm, let it be attacked by anyone, and put all the secrecy into a key that can be changed the moment it is lost.

Ignacy Lukasiewicz was a pharmacist in Lwow, then part of the Austrian empire, when he worked out how to distil the sticky rock oil sold locally as a folk medicine into a clean burning fuel. On 30 March 1853, he lit the first lamp built to burn it in the window of a Lwow pharmacy, and that July the same fuel lit an operating theatre during emergency surgery at the city hospital.

Kerosene burned brighter and far more cheaply than whale oil, which whaling had made increasingly scarce and expensive by mid century. Lukasiewicz went on to sink some of the world's first oil wells nearby, and within a generation kerosene lighting had spread across Europe and America, briefly making his corner of Galicia one of the centres of the emerging oil industry.

Vratislav II had ruled Bohemia as a duke under the Holy Roman Empire, one of several Premyslid princes who owed their title to the emperor rather than holding it outright. In 1085 the emperor Henry IV granted him the personal title of king, a reward for military support rather than a permanent elevation of the duchy itself.

The kingship did not pass automatically to Vratislav's successors, who reverted to the ducal title, and Bohemia only became a hereditary kingdom for good in 1198 under Ottokar I. Even so, 1085 marks the first time a Bohemian ruler wore a crown, the opening move in the process that built the medieval Czech state.

Unification in 1861 stitched together states that had been separate for over a thousand years, from the Kingdom of Sardinia to the small duchies of the north and, after Garibaldi's volunteer army swept south the previous year, the former Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Turin, the Sardinian capital, was the seat where the new national parliament first met that March.

That parliament proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II, already king of Sardinia, king of Italy, a title chosen rather than restyling him as a new first monarch, which signalled continuity with his own dynasty over any break with the past. Venice and Rome were still outside the new kingdom, held by Austria and by the Pope with French backing, and were not added until 1866 and 1870 respectively.

Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen spent the late 1850s at Heidelberg burning chemicals in Bunsen's newly improved gas burner and photographing the coloured lines each element produced through a prism, cataloguing which lines named which element. In 1859 Kirchhoff went further, showing that the dark lines Joseph von Fraunhofer had noticed crossing the Sun's spectrum decades earlier lined up with the bright lines of specific known elements.

That meant sunlight itself carried a chemical fingerprint of the gases in the Sun's outer layers, sodium and iron among them, readable from Earth without ever touching the object. The technique, spectroscopy, was quickly turned on other stars and later on distant galaxies, becoming the tool that told astronomers what everything in the universe is actually made of.

Arthur Evans bought the mound at Knossos outright before he ever put a spade in it, convinced by pottery fragments he had collected earlier that something large lay underneath. Digging began in March 1900, and within weeks his workers had exposed a sprawling complex of storerooms, halls and courtyards far bigger than anyone on Crete had expected.

Evans named the civilisation Minoan after the legendary King Minos and read the site through the myth, calling one wing the labyrinth and reconstructing corridors and columns in concrete based on his own guesses, restorations later archaeologists have criticised as overconfident. The undeciphered clay tablets he also unearthed, in a script he called Linear A and a related Linear B, took decades longer to make sense of than the building itself.

Georg von Reisswitz, a Prussian lieutenant, refined a game his father had already shown to the royal family into a version played on real contour maps with wooden blocks standing for units, dice governing outcomes, and an umpire adjudicating results the rules could not cover. In 1824 he demonstrated it to Prince Wilhelm, a corps commander who was impressed enough to push for its wider adoption.

The Prussian king ordered every regiment supplied with a set, and Reisswitz set up a workshop to produce them. Kriegsspiel became a standard tool for training officers in decision-making under uncertainty rather than rote drill, and its umpired, map-based format is usually credited as the ancestor of modern military wargaming.

Landsat 1 launched on 23 July 1972 as ERTS 1, a name NASA changed once it realised nobody could pronounce it. It circled the planet every 103 minutes in a polar orbit, crossing the same ground every 18 days so scientists could compare identical patches of land season after season rather than guess from scattered aerial photos.

The satellite carried a scanner tuned to wavelengths beyond human vision, letting analysts pick out crop stress, deforestation and glacier retreat invisible in ordinary colour photography. The Landsat programme has run continuously since, now on its ninth satellite, giving researchers an unbroken record of the same coastlines and forests stretching back more than five decades.

Emperor Yang of Sui had just moved the capital to Luoyang, and around 610 he marked the first full moon of the lunar year by lighting the city for days: strings of lanterns along the streets, musicians brought in from across the empire, and crowds allowed to stay out past the usual curfew. Later writers treated his court's extravagance as a symptom of the dynasty's coming collapse.

The festival itself was already old by then, tied to Han-dynasty rites honouring the god Taiyi, but Yang's Luoyang displays are the moment historians point to for fixing lanterns, music and public spectacle together as the form the holiday would keep. Lunar New Year celebrations across China still close with a lantern festival on that same full moon.

On 14 January 1506, a Roman named Felice de Fredis was digging in a vineyard near the ruins of Nero's Golden House when he struck a marble group showing the Trojan priest Laocoon and his two sons being crushed by serpents. Pope Julius II sent the architect Giuliano da Sangallo and the young Michelangelo to inspect the find within days, and the pope bought it almost immediately for the Vatican, where it still stands.

The group matched a description by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder of a statue he called without equal, which let scholars identify it on the spot rather than argue over its origin for decades. Its missing right arm, debated for centuries and restored several different ways, was finally settled in the 1950s when the original fragment turned up in a Roman stonemason's yard.

Leap seconds have been inserted into civil time since 1972 to keep clocks matched to Earth's slightly irregular rotation, which drifts against the atomic clocks defining official time. Each insertion has occasionally broken computer systems that were not built to expect a minute with 61 seconds, and the schedule cannot be set more than six months ahead.

In November 2022, delegates meeting in Versailles for the world's top time-keeping body voted to stop the practice, agreeing to let the gap between atomic and astronomical time grow beyond one second by 2035 rather than keep patching it. The exact replacement scheme is due for agreement at the next conference in 2026.

Around 1500, working in Venice on schemes to defend the city's harbour, Leonardo da Vinci sketched a diving suit of leather with a bell shaped mask, webbed gloves, and cane tubes running to the surface to let a diver breathe underwater. Notes beside the drawing describe fitting a wineskin so a diver could carry a reserve of air, and a knife for cutting the anchor lines or hulls of enemy ships.

Leonardo wrote that he was withholding some of these devices from publication because of the wickedness of men, who would use them for murder at the bottom of the sea, and he described sinking ships by boring holes below the waterline. The suit was never built in his lifetime as far as any surviving record shows, and it stayed a paper design among the notebooks he kept largely to himself.

Around 1495, Leonardo da Vinci sketched an automaton armoured knight in his notebooks, its limbs driven by internal cables, gears and pulleys rather than any hidden operator standing behind it. Drawings show mechanisms for the figure to sit upright, stand, turn its head and raise its arms, likely intended as a pageant piece for one of the elaborate court festivals Leonardo staged for his Milanese patron, Ludovico Sforza.

No original automaton survives, and it is unclear from the surviving pages whether a working version was ever built in Leonardo's lifetime or stayed a design on paper. Engineers and historians have since built working reconstructions from the notebook drawings, confirming that the mechanism as sketched is functional, which is more than can be said for several of Leonardo's other unrealised machines.

John Lethbridge was a wool merchant from Newton Abbot, not an engineer, when he built his diving machine in 1715: an airtight oak barrel about six feet long, with a viewing window and two leather-cuffed armholes, into which he climbed and lay face down while assistants lowered him from a boat. He had no air supply beyond what the barrel already held when it sealed.

He used the barrel to strip valuables from wrecks around the English and Dutch coasts, working shallow dives of limited duration but enough to recover cargo other salvagers could not reach. Word of his results eventually reached the East India Company, which arranged a demonstration on the Thames in 1720, and Lethbridge went on to work wrecks including the sunken East Indiaman Vansittart.

The Liechtenstein family had been wealthy Habsburg courtiers for generations without owning land that answered to nobody but the emperor, the qualification for a seat in the imperial diet. Prince Johann Adam bought Schellenberg in 1699 and Vaduz in 1712 for that reason alone, having never set foot in either.

On 23 January 1719, Emperor Charles VI merged the two purchases into a single Reichsfurstentum and named it Liechtenstein, after the family rather than the place. No prince lived there until 1842. The country that resulted, still ruled by that family, is now one of the smallest sovereign states in Europe and the only one named for its owners rather than its geography.

Michael Ventris first heard the archaeologist Arthur Evans lecture on the mysterious Cretan tablets in 1936, when he was fourteen. He trained and worked as an architect through the 1940s, treating the script as a private puzzle he pursued in his spare time using grids of sound-values he built up from patterns in the symbols rather than any known language.

In June 1952 he announced on BBC radio that the script, previously assumed to be a lost Minoan tongue, recorded an archaic form of Greek some five hundred years older than Homer. The classicist John Chadwick helped confirm and extend the decipherment, and Ventris gave up architecture entirely, though he died in a car accident only four years later, in 1956.

In 1417, London's mayor Henry Barton ordered householders on the main streets to hang out lanterns on dark winter nights, from the feast of All Hallows to Candlemas, when there was no moon to light the way. The order was aimed at a city with no public lighting of its own, where robbery and simple collision were constant risks after dusk, and it made each household responsible for a small stretch of the street outside its own door.

The rule was patchily kept and repeated by later mayors over the following two centuries, evidence that compliance never became automatic. It is one of the earliest known attempts by an English city to legislate street lighting at all, well before oil lamps or any paid lamplighter existed to do the job instead.

Joseph Bazalgette did not set out to stop cholera. London built his brick sewers to stop the smell, after the Great Stink of 1858 drove MPs from the Commons chamber and finally freed the money that years of cholera deaths had failed to unlock. The 1865 opening, at Abbey Mills pumping station, ran interceptor sewers roughly parallel to the Thames, carrying waste east past the built-up city before releasing it.

Cholera was still widely blamed on foul air rather than contaminated water when the scheme was designed. It worked anyway, because removing the sewage removed the water-borne bacterium along with the smell that everyone thought was the real danger. London had no major cholera outbreak after the network opened, an accidental proof of John Snow's theory that the engineers themselves did not fully accept.

Sailors could fix their latitude easily from the sun's height, but longitude, position east or west, had no equally simple check, and ships that misjudged it ran aground or starved searching for land that was not where they thought. Parliament passed the Longitude Act in 1714 after a string of naval disasters, offering up to 20,000 pounds for a workable method.

The problem reduced to keeping precise time at sea, since longitude could be calculated from the difference between local time and time at a known reference point, if a clock could survive months of pitching, damp and temperature swings without losing more than a few seconds a day. That challenge was eventually solved by Yorkshire carpenter John Harrison, whose marine chronometers won the prize decades later.

On the evening of 23 November 1407, Louis of Orleans left a house in Paris where he had visited the queen and was ambushed on the rue Vieille du Temple by a gang of masked men who hacked him from his mule and left his body in the street. John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, admitted within days that he had ordered it, and a Paris theologian was found to argue publicly that killing a tyrant was lawful.

Louis and John were cousins and rivals for control of the mad king Charles VI's government, and the murder split France into Armagnac and Burgundian factions that fought a civil war for decades. That split let Henry V of England exploit French disunity, an opening that led directly to Agincourt eight years later.

In 1966 the engineers Charles Kao and George Hockham argued that glass fibre could carry light-based signals over long distances if impurities in the glass could be cut enough, since it was contamination, not the glass itself, that scattered and absorbed the light. Existing fibre at the time lost most of its signal within a few metres, far too lossy to be useful for communication.

Researchers at Corning Glass Works, led by Robert Maurer, Donald Keck and Peter Schultz, met that target in 1970 by drawing fibre from ultra-pure fused silica doped with titanium, achieving losses low enough to send light usefully over a kilometre. The breakthrough turned optical fibre from a laboratory curiosity into the basis for the telecommunications networks that would later carry the internet.

Lu Yu was an orphan raised by Buddhist monks who taught him to prepare tea for temple ceremonies, and he spent much of his adult life travelling the tea-growing regions of Tang China before writing it all down. His Classic of Tea, finished around 760, covers the soil tea grows best in, how to pick and roast the leaf, the right water, and the etiquette of serving it to guests.

Nothing that thorough on the subject existed before it, and Lu Yu became known after his death as the Sage of Tea, with shrines built to him by tea merchants. His three-part division of preparation, brewing and drinking shaped the increasingly formal tea culture that spread from Tang China into Japan, where it later fed into the tea ceremony.

The estuary at Luoyang, near Quanzhou in Fujian, had currents too strong and a bed too soft for ordinary stone piers. Work began in 1053 under the scholar official Cai Xiang, and by the time it finished in 1059 the bridge stretched roughly 730 metres, one of the longest stone beam bridges built anywhere up to that point.

Cai Xiang's solution to the shifting seabed was to seed the pier foundations with oysters, whose shells cemented the loose stone into a solid mass as they grew. It is the earliest known case of a builder deliberately using a living organism to reinforce a structure, and colonies of oysters were still clinging to the piers centuries later.

Luxembourg's independence in 1839 did not come from a revolt or a battle. It came from the great powers redrawing a map to settle a dispute left over from the Belgian Revolution of 1830, when the largely French speaking western part of the old Grand Duchy had joined breakaway Belgium. The Treaty of London confirmed that split, carving off the eastern remainder as a smaller, separate state.

What remained kept the name and the ruling House of Orange-Nassau, still joined to the Netherlands only through the person of the king, and joined the German Confederation for defence. The borders drawn in London that year are, with minor adjustments, still Luxembourg's borders today, making 1839 rather than any later date the country's real founding moment.

Ma Jun worked as a mechanical engineer at the Wei court during the Three Kingdoms period, a time of near-constant war between rival states that put a premium on any device that could help an army navigate unfamiliar ground. His south-pointing chariot carried a wooden figure on top with an arm outstretched toward the south.

No magnet or compass needle was involved. A train of differential gears linked to the chariot's wheels sensed every turn the vehicle made and turned the figure by the same amount in the opposite direction, so it kept facing one direction regardless of the road. The device does not survive, and everything known about it comes from written descriptions later reconstructed by scholars.

The Straits of Mackinac separate Michigan's two peninsulas with open water funnelling wind and ice between Lake Michigan and Lake Huron, which had made a fixed crossing there a byword for impossible engineering for decades. Ferries carried cars across, with waits that stretched to hours on holiday weekends, until construction on a suspension bridge began in 1954.

The Mackinac Bridge opened to traffic on 1 November 1957, stretching about 26,372 feet, roughly five miles, between anchorages. It was the longest suspension bridge in the world by that measure until Japan's Akashi Kaikyo Bridge overtook it in 1998, and it remains the longest in the western hemisphere, still carrying nearly all road traffic between Michigan's two halves.

A church floor in Madaba, in modern Jordan, once carried more than two million coloured stones set into a map of the Holy Land stretching from Lebanon to the Nile delta. Only about a third of it survives, uncovered when the church was rebuilt in 1884, but its central panel, an oval street plan of Jerusalem, is the earliest surviving depiction of the city's layout.

The mosaic names dozens of towns in Greek and shows real buildings: the Damascus Gate, the Holy Sepulchre, a colonnaded main street running through the walls. Its date is fixed between two known events it does and does not include, a church dedicated in 542 that appears and later Jerusalem buildings that do not, placing it close to 560.

The game's own origin stories, a bored Confucius or Ming-dynasty sailors, have no evidence behind them. What survives instead is a set of card games played around the Yangtze delta cities of Shanghai and Ningbo in the 1870s, built on drawing and discarding to complete matched sets, the mechanic that mahjong kept when it moved from paper to tile.

Carving the same games into tiles made them sturdier, shuffleable and harder to mark for cheating, and the new form spread quickly along the same trade routes that had carried the card games. By the early twentieth century mahjong had reached treaty ports and, from there, American and European parlours, where manufacturers added their own rule variants and lacquered sets.

Malta had passed between Phoenician, Roman, Arab, Norman, Aragonese, Hospitaller and French control before Britain took the islands in 1800, drawn by the deep harbour at Valletta that made Malta a naval base guarding the route to Suez and India. British rule lasted 164 years, through two world wars in which Malta's dockyards and civilians endured heavy bombing.

Independence came on 21 September 1964 under the Malta Independence Act, passed by the British parliament after a referendum on the new constitution earlier that year. Malta kept Elizabeth II as head of state, represented by a Maltese governor-general, and did not become a republic outright until a further, separate change a decade later, in 1974.

Mamluk Cairo built glass lamps meant to be seen lit from below, hung by chains in dozens along a mosque or madrasa's ceiling so their enamelled Arabic inscriptions glowed against the dark. Glassmakers built up colour by fusing powdered enamel and gold leaf onto the surface in multiple firings, a technique demanding enough that only a handful of workshops mastered it.

Many lamps bore the name and blazon of the sultan or emir who endowed the building, turning light itself into a form of public record. European collectors and later museums prized these lamps highly once trade and travel brought them west, and surviving examples from the 1330s remain among the most sought-after objects of Mamluk decorative art.

The Great Pyramid's original entrance had been sealed and hidden for over three thousand years when the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun's workmen, hunting for treasure around 820, gave up looking for it and simply tunnelled straight into the north face. Where they broke through solid limestone core blocks they could not push past the granite plugs blocking the ascending passage above, so they dug around them instead.

Their forced tunnel is still the passage visitors use to enter the pyramid today. Arab chroniclers writing generations later disagree on whether al-Ma'mun found treasure, a mummy, or nothing at all inside, and none of the earliest accounts even names 820 as the year, a date modern historians reconstructed rather than found stated outright.

Mancala is a family of games, not one game: two players sow seeds or stones around rows of pits, capturing an opponent's row by counting a chain to a set number. Boards cut into rock at sites in Africa and the Near East, some dated to around 1000 BCE, are the earliest physical evidence, though any older wooden boards would not have survived.

Because the boards are plain pits rather than inscribed objects, dating and attributing them is difficult, and claims for an older origin site are argued over. What is not disputed is the game's reach: variants under different names are still played from Senegal to Southeast Asia, among the most widely spread board games anywhere.

Pneumonic plague spread through Manchuria's rail towns over the winter of 1910 to 1911, killing roughly sixty thousand people before it was stopped. It spread through the air between people, unlike the flea-borne bubonic form, which made crowded railway carriages and marmot-fur traders' lodgings especially dangerous places to be.

The Cambridge-trained doctor Wu Lien-teh was sent to Harbin to run the response. He pushed cotton-and-gauze masks on medical staff and later the public, imposed rail cordons and travel quarantines, and, against local custom, ordered mass cremation of the frozen unburied dead once the ground proved too hard to dig. The epidemic ended within months, and Wu's methods shaped China's later public health institutions.

Marat was in a medicinal bath on 13 July 1793 when he received her, treating a skin condition that kept him working from the tub with a board across it as a desk. Charlotte Corday, a young royalist sympathiser from Normandy, had gained entry by promising names of Girondin fugitives, then stabbed him once in the chest with a kitchen knife she had bought that morning.

She made no attempt to flee and was arrested at the scene, tried within four days, and guillotined on 17 July. Jacques-Louis David's painting of Marat dead in the bath, made within months, shaped how the killing is remembered far more than any account of Corday herself, who left a written justification insisting she had acted alone.

Frank Rosenblatt built the Mark I Perceptron at Cornell in 1958 as a physical machine rather than software, wired with 400 photocells arranged in a 20 by 20 grid to stand in for a retina, connected through adjustable potentiometers that a motor turned to strengthen or weaken each connection as the machine was shown examples.

Fed enough labelled images, the perceptron could learn on its own to sort simple shapes without being told the rules for telling them apart, an early demonstration of what would later be called a neural network. The New York Times reported that the Navy expected it to walk, talk and reproduce itself, a claim the machine's actual, narrow abilities never came close to justifying.

The ship Grand-Saint-Antoine reached Marseille from Levantine ports in May 1720 carrying silk, cotton and several crew already dead of plague. Harbour officials, wary of losing a lucrative cargo, let it dock instead of holding it in quarantine at the offshore lazaretto, and the disease came ashore within days.

At its worst the city buried close to a thousand people a day, and estimates for Marseille alone run as high as forty five thousand dead, roughly half its population, with the wider region of Provence losing tens of thousands more before it burned out in 1722. It was the last time bubonic plague killed on that scale in western Europe.

When Edward VI died in 1553, his council tried to bypass Mary, his elder half-sister and a Catholic, by installing Lady Jane Grey instead. Jane held the throne for nine days before public and noble support swung behind Mary, who entered London that August and became the first woman to rule England in her own right rather than as a king's wife or regent.

Mary set about reversing her father's and brother's break with Rome, restoring papal authority and reviving the heresy laws that Edward's government had let lapse. Under those laws roughly 280 Protestants were burned over the following years, earning her the name Bloody Mary in later Protestant memory, while her marriage to Philip II of Spain drew England into his wars without producing the heir she needed.

The maps were sealed in a lacquer box inside a Han tomb at Mawangdui, near Changsha in modern Hunan province, likely belonging to a son of Li Cang, ruler of the Changsha kingdom, and buried around 168 BC. Excavation only began in 1972, so the maps were unread for over two thousand years before archaeologists opened the box.

One map covers the region south of Changsha, marking rivers, settlements and mountains with a consistency of scale that surprised historians who assumed such precision was centuries later. A second map lays out military garrisons along the kingdom's frontier, giving historians a rare direct view of Han defensive planning rather than a later, secondhand description of it.

Through the mid-twentieth century most Mayanists, following the influential epigrapher J. Eric Thompson, treated Maya glyphs as records of astronomy and ritual calendars rather than history, on the assumption that Maya inscriptions never named actual rulers. Tatiana Proskouriakoff, working at Harvard's Peabody Museum, doubted this while studying stelae from the site of Piedras Negras in Guatemala.

In a 1960 paper she showed that repeating glyph groups on the stelae matched the spacing of a human lifespan, and that dates on them clustered around what looked like births, accessions to power, and deaths of named individuals. Her reading opened the glyphs to full decipherment as dynastic history, work that continued for decades and eventually let scholars name and date real Maya kings.

Wolfgang von Kempelen built the Turk to impress Empress Maria Theresa after boasting he could improve on a magic show he had just watched at court. It debuted in 1770: a wooden figure in Ottoman dress, seated behind a cabinet, moving chess pieces with a mechanical arm and beating nearly every opponent put in front of it, Napoleon and Benjamin Franklin included.

The cabinet's gears and levers were a distraction. A cramped human chess player hid inside, sliding along rails as the doors were opened to prove the compartment empty, and steered the arm using magnets and a peep hole under the board. The deception held for decades across Europe and America before it was finally exposed in print after the machine burned in an 1854 fire.

The Meio earthquake struck off Japan's Nankai coast on 20 September 1498, an estimated magnitude near 8.6 that sent a tsunami into Kamakura, then a former shogunal capital already past its political peak. Reported death tolls vary enormously between contemporary and later accounts, from a few thousand up to over 40,000, a spread that reflects how unevenly the disaster was recorded rather than any precise count.

The wave swept away the wooden hall that had sheltered Kamakura's bronze Great Buddha since the thirteenth century, leaving the statue itself standing largely undamaged in the open air. By 1498 Kyoto held political power rather than Kamakura, and no funds arrived to rebuild the hall, so the Buddha has sat exposed to weather ever since, an accident of neglect rather than a deliberate design choice.

The tablet is not a secret alphabet but a scrambled spelling. A scribe writing a glaze recipe around 1500 BCE at Nippur swapped syllabic signs for rarer ones carrying the same sound, so a reader had to already know the pronunciation to decode the words. That trick, not a new script, makes it the earliest cipher known to survive.

The recipe itself listed minerals and firing steps for colouring pottery glaze, knowledge potters guarded as a trade secret. Disguising the cuneiform kept a rival craftsman from reading the formula even if the tablet fell into his hands, protecting it through obscurity rather than any lock or seal.

Meton of Athens set up a sundial on the Pnyx and, working with Euctemon, tracked solstices and lunar months closely enough to notice that 19 solar years come out almost exactly equal to 235 lunar months, a gap of only a couple of hours. He announced the cycle in Athens in 432 BC, timed to the summer solstice.

The cycle let a lunar calendar stay aligned with the seasons without slow drift, by inserting seven extra months across each nineteen-year span rather than guessing year by year. Athens never fully adopted Meton's scheme for civic use, but the same ratio resurfaced centuries later in the calculation of Easter's date, still called the Metonic cycle.

Albert Michelson and Edward Morley built their interferometer expecting to measure Earth's motion through a stationary ether, the medium physicists assumed light needed to wave through. Mounted on a slab of sandstone floating in mercury to damp vibration, the device split a beam of light, sent the halves down perpendicular paths, and looked for a shift in the pattern when they recombined as Earth turned through the supposed ether wind.

The 1887 result at Case School in Cleveland was a null: no shift, far below what the ether theory required, however the apparatus was rotated or the season changed. Repeated attempts to explain the null away only made the ether harder to defend, and the result is remembered now mainly for the theory it helped clear the ground for, Einstein's special relativity.

Mindaugas had already spent years killing or exiling rival dukes before he accepted baptism in 1251 and asked Pope Innocent IV for a crown. The pope agreed, and on 6 July 1253 papal legates anointed Mindaugas and his wife Morta at a ceremony whose exact site is still argued over, somewhere near Vilnius or Novogrudok.

The gambit was political as much as religious: a crown made Lithuania a recognised Christian kingdom, not a pagan target for the Teutonic Knights' crusading claims. It did not last. Mindaugas was assassinated by rival nobles in 1263, Lithuania reverted to paganism, and no ruler after him used the royal title again until the modern republic revived the date as a national holiday.

Bubonic plague had been killing over a thousand Muscovites a day by September 1771 when crowds gathered around an icon of the Virgin at the Barbarian Gate, believing it could cure them. Archbishop Ambrosius, trying to stop a crowd that spread the disease faster than it prayed it away, had the icon moved and its donation box sealed.

On 15 September the crowd stormed the Kremlin, wrecked the archbishop's residence and killed him the next day. Catherine the Great sent troops under Grigory Orlov to put the riot down; the wider epidemic, one of the last major outbreaks of plague in Europe, is thought to have killed roughly a third of Moscow's population before it ended.

Saint-Pierre's authorities kept residents in the city as Mount Pelee rumbled through April 1902, partly to avoid disrupting an election and partly because nobody nearby had seen a pyroclastic flow before and did not know to fear one specifically. On the morning of 8 May a superheated cloud of gas and ash raced down the mountain's slope and reached the port town within about a minute.

Nearly all of Saint-Pierre's roughly 28,000 residents died, most from the heat itself rather than from ash or falling debris; ships anchored in the harbour caught fire and sank. A handful of survivors were found, including a prisoner in a partly underground cell. The disaster gave volcanology the term pyroclastic flow and a clear demonstration of how fast such a flow moves.

Just after two in the morning on 10 February 1567, an explosion tore apart the Kirk o' Field house in Edinburgh where Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, was staying. Two barrels of gunpowder had been packed into a room beneath his lodging. His body and that of a servant were found in the garden outside, apparently strangled rather than killed by the blast, suggesting he had escaped the building before it collapsed.
