Suspicion fell immediately on the Earl of Bothwell, and by extension on Mary, Queen of Scots, whose marriage to Darnley had already broken down. Bothwell stood trial and was acquitted, then married Mary within three months, a decision Scottish nobles used to force her abdication the following year. No account of who planned the killing has ever been settled beyond dispute.

Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, dug into the ruined ziggurat of Ur around 550 BCE while restoring it, searching for the temple's original foundation deposits. He found inscribed cylinders naming earlier builders, including Ur-Nammu, and had his own account of the discovery buried inside the walls he rebuilt.

He did the same at the Ebabbar temple in Sippar, uncovering an inscription of the much older king Naram-Sin and estimating, wrongly but seriously, how many centuries had passed since it was buried. Historians count these digs among the earliest deliberate excavations aimed at recovering the past rather than reusing building material.

John Napier was a Scottish laird who spent twenty years on the side project that made his name, working it out by hand with no algebra beyond what he invented for the purpose. His Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio, published in 1614, gave astronomers and navigators a table that turned lengthy multiplication and division into simple addition and subtraction.

Henry Briggs, a London mathematician, read the book, travelled to Edinburgh to meet Napier, and spent the rest of his career refining the tables into the base-10 logarithms still taught today. Napier never saw that version finished. He also invented Napier's bones, a set of numbered rods for mechanical multiplication, which spread further and faster than the logarithms themselves.

Lake Nemi, a flooded volcanic crater south of Rome, was known to hold two enormous barges built as floating palaces for the emperor Caligula, roughly seventy metres long and lost since antiquity. In July 1535 the engineer Francesco de Marchi hired Guglielmo de Lorena to go down and find them, using a bell of Guglielmo's own design that rested on the diver's shoulders and trapped air around his head.

The bell was small enough to hold only a few minutes of breathable air, but it had a mechanism for venting used air while keeping the water out, letting Guglielmo work submerged far longer than a single breath allowed. He never explained how it worked. De Marchi had sworn an oath of secrecy, and the two brought up marble and bronze fragments from the barges without disclosing the device that got them there.

Coca-Cola introduced a reformulated, sweeter recipe on 23 April 1985 after blind taste tests suggested drinkers preferred it, and quietly retired the 99-year-old original in the same move. The company had been losing ground to Pepsi's sweeter cola and treated the switch as a straightforward fix to a market research problem.

The reaction was fury rather than gratitude. Tens of thousands of complaint calls and letters poured in, some from drinkers who said the old formula tasted like home rather than a beverage. Coca-Cola brought the original recipe back on 10 July 1985, marketed as Coca-Cola Classic, just 79 days after New Coke launched, in what became a textbook case of underestimating brand loyalty.

The Niagara Falls Power Company's 1895 station settled a fight that had run for years between Thomas Edison's direct current and George Westinghouse's alternating current. Westinghouse won the contract, using Nikola Tesla's patented AC induction motor design, partly because AC could be transformed to high voltage for the journey and stepped back down at the far end without the huge losses DC suffered over distance.

The station's generators sent power some twenty miles to Buffalo, lighting streets and running factories far from the turbines that made the electricity. It was the demonstration the AC side needed: cheap, distant power was possible, and within a few years AC transmission became the standard that electrical grids were built on.

On the night of 10 to 11 December 969, John Tzimiskes and three fellow conspirators crossed the storm tossed Bosphorus and reached the Boukoleon Palace, where the emperor's own wife Theophano lowered a basket on a rope to bring them inside. She had persuaded Nikephoros not to lock his bedchamber door.

A eunuch pointed out where the emperor lay asleep on the floor, having given up his bed for austerity's sake. The attackers struck him awake with a sword, and Tzimiskes kicked him before finishing him. Nikephoros's guards, rushing in on the noise, are said to have stopped short at the sight of his severed head. Tzimiskes took the throne within days.

The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art survives as a collection of practical problems: dividing land, taxing grain, sizing canals, split into nine chapters by subject. It was compiled from older material by unnamed authors, then expanded with a commentary by Liu Hui in the third century CE that explained why the methods worked rather than just stating them.

Among its methods is fangcheng, a rule for solving several equations with several unknowns at once by arranging their coefficients in a grid and cancelling terms, the same idea western mathematics would later call Gaussian elimination. Red and black counting rods let the text represent negative numbers directly, well before European mathematics accepted them.

Nine Men's Morris boards from around 1400 BCE are cut, not drawn: grids of three concentric squares scratched into the roofing slabs at the temple of Kurna in Egypt, where workers waiting out slow hours scored a game into stone rather than papyrus. Players moved counters along the lines, trying to land three in a row.

The Kurna boards are only the earliest surviving examples, not proof the game began there. Similar grids turn up cut into temple steps and floors across the ancient Mediterranean, Rome included, wherever masons or guards had stone underfoot and time on their hands. The rules travelled without needing a single point of origin.

Austen Henry Layard was a broke young traveller with no formal training when he began digging at the mound of Kuyunjik, opposite Mosul, in the 1840s, funded on a shoestring by the British ambassador in Constantinople. Local workers had already found stone fragments there, but Layard's trenches in 1847 struck the palace of the Assyrian king Sennacherib, buried and forgotten for over two thousand years.

He shipped enormous winged bull statues and slabs of battle relief down the Tigris on rafts and across the desert by cart to reach the sea, a feat nearly as remarkable as the finds themselves. The reliefs, now largely in the British Museum, gave Europe its first direct look at Assyrian court life and warfare, and the site later also yielded the clay tablets that let cuneiform be checked and confirmed.

Nizam al-Mulk had run the Seljuk empire's administration for three decades, founding the Nizamiyyah colleges that trained its bureaucrats and shaping policy under two sultans. In October 1092 he was stabbed to death near Nihavand by a man disguised as a Sufi petitioner, on the orders of the Nizari Ismaili leader Hassan i Sabbah from the mountain fortress of Alamut.

The Nizaris used targeted, individual killings rather than open rebellion against a far larger Seljuk state, and their agents became known to Crusader chroniclers as hashishin, a name that passed into European languages as assassin. Nizam al-Mulk is usually counted as the sect's first prominent victim, killed within weeks of the sultan he served.

Nikolai Lobachevsky published his geometry in 1829 in a Kazan University journal few outside Russia read, working out what followed if Euclid's parallel postulate, that exactly one line through a point never meets a given line, was simply false. He built a consistent system, later called hyperbolic geometry, where infinitely many such parallels exist.

Janos Bolyai reached similar conclusions independently around the same years in Hungary, and Gauss had worked out much of it privately without publishing, fearing the reaction it would provoke. Only decades later, once Bernhard Riemann and others showed the new geometries were as sound as Euclid's, did mathematicians accept that space need not obey the axioms taught since antiquity.

Offa ruled Mercia for nearly forty years and dominated the other Anglo-Saxon kingdoms so completely that he struck his own gold coinage and had his daughters married into rival royal houses. Around 785 he had a bank and ditch raised along much of the border with the Welsh kingdoms, running roughly 130 kilometres from the Dee estuary toward the Severn.

The dyke was never a continuous wall and did not need to be; long stretches used rivers and existing ridges to fill the gaps, with the earthwork itself concentrated where the ground gave no natural barrier. Much of it still stands, and a long-distance footpath now follows its line, making it one of the largest surviving works of Anglo-Saxon England.

Heinrich Olbers set out the puzzle formally in 1823, though he was refining an argument earlier astronomers, including Johannes Kepler, had already raised: if the universe is infinite, static and evenly filled with stars, every line of sight should eventually end on a stellar surface, making the whole sky as bright as the Sun.

Olbers guessed the answer was dust absorbing distant starlight, which turned out to be wrong, since absorbed light would simply heat the dust until it glowed as brightly. The real resolution came only with an expanding universe of finite age: light from the most distant stars has not had time to reach us, and the universe's youth, not its dust, is what keeps the night dark.

Britain's Board of Ordnance began a national survey in 1791, prompted partly by fears of French invasion and a need for maps good enough to move troops on, and partly by an earlier boundary dispute with France that had shown how poor existing charts were. Work started from a baseline measured across Hounslow Heath, chosen because it was flat and open enough to lay a chain accurately.

Surveyors triangulated outward from that baseline across the whole country, publishing the first one-inch-to-the-mile sheets over the following decades. The organisation that grew from that survey, still called the Ordnance Survey, remains Britain's national mapping agency more than two centuries later, long after the invasion threat that started it had passed.

Pancho Villa had accepted a government pardon in 1920 and settled on a ranch at Canutillo, running it as a colony for his former soldiers. On 20 July 1923 he was driving into the town of Parral in his Dodge touring car when gunmen firing from a house on the route killed him and several companions.

The assassination was never conclusively tied to a single sponsor, though suspicion fell on local and national political figures wary of Villa re-entering public life ahead of the 1924 presidential succession. One of the ambush party, Jesus Salas Barraza, was tried, convicted, and served under a year before receiving a commission in the army.

On 20 February 1943 a Purepecha farmer named Dionisio Pulido was burning brush in his cornfield near Uruapan when the ground swelled, cracked open, and hissed sulphur smoke. Within a day the fissure had thrown up a cinder cone roughly 50 metres high. Pulido tried to protect his plot with a shovel before giving up and fleeing with his family.

The cone kept growing for nine years, reaching about 424 metres, while lava and ash buried the villages of Paricutin and San Juan Parangaricutiro. No one died in the eruption itself, though the displacement scattered thousands of residents permanently. Because it was watched from its first hour, geologists got a rare full record of a volcano's entire birth and adolescence.

Etienne Boileau, provost of Paris under Louis IX, faced a problem that had nothing to do with wax: trade rules in the city existed only as oral custom, passed master to apprentice, and disputes had no written text to settle them. Around 1268 he asked each Parisian craft to write down its own statutes and compiled the results into the Livre des metiers, the Book of Trades.

Among roughly a hundred crafts recorded were the tallow chandlers, who rendered animal fat into cheap everyday candles, and the wax chandlers who supplied the costlier light burned in churches and wealthy houses. Their entries fixed apprenticeship terms, quality checks and who could sell what, giving Paris its earliest surviving written regulation of the trades that lit it.

Louis XIV appointed Gabriel Nicolas de la Reynie as Paris's first lieutenant general of police in March 1667, giving him a mandate to make the streets safer that went well beyond simply hiring more officers. Among his measures was ordering metal-and-glass lanterns hung on poles above the main streets and asking residents to keep windows lit with candles or oil lamps after dark.

By 1668 nearly three thousand of these lanterns were burning across the city, a scale no other European capital had attempted, meant to strip criminals of the darkness they relied on rather than to simply light the way for pedestrians. The measure is the origin most often given for Paris's later nickname, the City of Light, though the phrase would come to mean something closer to intellectual brilliance than street lamps.

On Easter Sunday, 26 April 1478, during High Mass in Florence's cathedral, conspirators from the rival Pazzi banking family and allies of Pope Sixtus IV attacked Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici at the ringing of the sanctus bell. Giuliano was stabbed repeatedly and died where he fell; Lorenzo, wounded in the neck, drew his sword, vaulted a low barrier and escaped through the sacristy with the help of friends.

Florence's response was immediate and brutal. Conspirators were hunted down and hanged from the windows of the Palazzo della Signoria within days, including the archbishop of Pisa, who had helped plan the attack. The failed plot left Lorenzo more securely in control of Florence than before, while Sixtus IV, implicated in the plot, placed the city under a papal interdict and pushed it into a two year war.

Pei Xiu was a minister under the Jin dynasty after the fall of Wei, and used his access to court archives to revise a large regional map of the empire that he judged inaccurate. His preface to that revised atlas, rather than the map itself, is what survives, and it is the earliest Chinese text to state cartographic principles explicitly.

He listed six rules a mapmaker had to hold together: consistent scale, a grid for measuring distance, correct orientation of features to each other, accounting for the actual shape of terrain, the true length of roads, and adjustment for the curve of hills and rivers. The map he drew from them is lost, but the six principles were cited by Chinese cartographers for centuries afterward.

Petrus Peregrinus was a French soldier and scholar who, in 1269, wrote the earliest surviving treatise devoted entirely to magnetism, the Epistola de magnete. He carved a lodestone into a sphere, laid a needle flat on its surface at different points and marked the direction it swung until the marks traced circles converging on two opposite points.

He called those points poles by analogy with the Earth's own axis, the first clear statement that a magnet has two poles that behave differently towards each other. The letter also describes a pivoted compass needle housed for use at sea, a genuine improvement on floating needles, three centuries before William Gilbert's more famous study of magnetism built on the same groundwork.

Peter III had ruled Russia for six months when his wife Catherine, backed by the Imperial Guard regiments he had alienated by favouring Prussia and cutting their privileges, had him arrested at his summer palace in June 1762 and forced his abdication within days.

He was moved under guard to the estate of Ropsha, where he died on 17 July, officially of haemorrhoidal colic. Catherine's own circle, including the guards officer left in charge of him, gave differing and contradictory accounts of a fight, leaving the exact cause disputed while the outcome was not: Catherine took the throne as Catherine the Great.

Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, a Swiss traveller working for the African Association under the name Sheikh Ibrahim, learned Arabic and Islamic law well enough to pass as a pilgrim among the Bedouin who controlled the Wadi Musa gorge. In August 1812 he persuaded a local guide to lead him through the narrow Siq, telling him he wished to sacrifice a goat at what he had heard was a tomb inside.

What he found was the rock-cut facade of the Khazneh, the centre of a Nabataean city carved into sandstone cliffs and abandoned to Bedouin use for centuries after trade routes shifted away from it. Burckhardt wrote up the discovery in a journal published after his death, and Petra became a fixed destination for European travellers within a generation.

Petrarch spent years hunting monastic libraries for manuscripts abandoned since antiquity, convinced that classical Rome held wisdom the medieval schools had buried under commentary. In 1345, searching the chapter library of Verona cathedral, he came across a manuscript of Cicero's letters to his friend Atticus, personal correspondence rather than the polished oratory Cicero was already known for.

Reading a great Roman statesman's private doubts and grievances gave Petrarch a model for a self scrutinising, individual voice that his own letters and sonnets then imitated. Historians of the Renaissance treat this find, one of several Petrarch made, as the moment humanist scholarship turned from admiring antiquity at a distance to reading it as one person addressing another.

The map that survives is a medieval copy, made around 1200 from a Roman original, of the empire's road network stretched into an impossibly long, thin strip nearly seven metres long and only about thirty four centimetres tall. Rivers, mountains and seas are squeezed to fit the shape, which is why the geography looks so distorted next to any modern map.

What it actually records are way stations along the roads and the distances between them, information a traveller or courier using the imperial post could use directly. It survived in a library at Worms until a scholar named Konrad Peutinger acquired it in the early sixteenth century, and it is now the only substantial map of the Roman road system to survive at all.

Phil Zimmermann released Pretty Good Privacy in 1991 as free software, built partly from RSA's public-key method, so that ordinary people, not just governments and corporations, could encrypt email strongly enough that even well-resourced attackers could not readily break it. He wrote it, by his own account, out of concern for activists and dissidents whose communications could otherwise be read.

Because PGP used strong cryptography and spread online beyond American borders, the United States government opened a criminal investigation into Zimmermann under export control laws that treated powerful encryption like a weapon. The case dragged on for three years before being dropped in 1996 without charges, by which point PGP had already become a fixture of digital privacy tools.

Philip II was killed in 336 BC at Aegae during festivities for his daughter's wedding, stabbed by Pausanias, one of his own royal bodyguards, as he walked into the theatre. Pausanias was cut down by other guards while fleeing, before he could be questioned, which left his motive a matter of ancient speculation rather than confirmed record.

Ancient historians offered rival explanations, from a personal grievance over an unpunished assault to a wider court conspiracy possibly involving Persia or rivals close to the throne, and no version is provable from what survives. The immediate effect is not in doubt: Philip's twenty-year-old son Alexander was proclaimed king within days, inheriting an army and a kingdom Philip had spent his reign building.

Plzen's brewers had a public reason to want a new beer: in 1838, townsfolk publicly dumped dozens of barrels of the local ale, judging it undrinkable. The city built a new civic brewery and hired a Bavarian brewer, Josef Groll, who brought bottom-fermenting lager yeast and a technique for pale malting that had just spread from Britain.

Groll's first batch, tapped in October 1842, came out a clear golden colour nobody in Bohemia had produced before, in a country used to darker, cloudier beers. Improved glassware let drinkers actually see that clarity, and the style, sold as Pilsner, was copied so widely across Europe and beyond that the city name became shorthand for an entire category of beer.

Charles Wheatstone, already known for early telegraph work, devised his letter pair cipher around 1854, but it carries a different man's name because his friend Lord Playfair was the one who pushed it in front of the government. Wheatstone reportedly demonstrated it to officials at the Foreign Office, only to be told it was too complicated for their clerks to learn.

Playfair's advocacy eventually won the cipher a place in British military use, and it saw real service in the Boer War and the First World War, encrypting messages by substituting pairs of letters according to their position on a five by five grid built from a keyword. It was not unbreakable, but it was far sturdier against casual attack than the simple letter for letter substitutions officers had relied on before.

Playing cards had circulated in the Islamic world for generations before Europe took any documented notice of them. The change came abruptly: city councils across the continent began banning or taxing card games within a few years of each other, suggesting the cards themselves, likely carried through Mamluk Egypt and Mediterranean trade, spread with unusual speed once they arrived.

In 1377 a Dominican friar named John of Rheinfelden wrote a treatise in Basel describing a fifty-two card deck of ten numbered cards and three court figures, the earliest detailed European account of how the game was played. Florence's city records mention card playing that same year, and by 1380 cards are attested in Basel, Regensburg, Brabant, Paris and Barcelona alike.

Poggio Bracciolini was a papal secretary who spent his idle stretches at the Council of Constance combing German monastery libraries for classical texts the Church had let rot. In 1417, at a monastery usually identified as Fulda, he found a manuscript of Lucretius's On the Nature of Things, a poem arguing that the world is made of atoms moving through empty space, with no gods intervening and no soul that survives the body.

Poggio had it copied and sent to Italy; that copy is lost, but it was copied again, and one of those descendants survives today in Florence. The poem's account of a universe without divine oversight unsettled and fascinated readers across the Renaissance, feeding arguments that would later trouble Galileo's contemporaries and, further off still, Enlightenment materialists.

Henri Poincare posed the question in 1904, and for the rest of the twentieth century it resisted every attempt to settle it, becoming one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems with a million dollar reward. In 2002 and 2003, Grigori Perelman posted three papers to an online preprint server rather than a journal, sketching a proof built on Richard Hamilton's earlier work on Ricci flow.

It took other mathematicians several years to verify the argument in full, since Perelman had left gaps for others to fill rather than writing every step out. He was awarded the Fields Medal in 2006 and the million dollar Clay Prize in 2010, and turned both down, saying he had already decided what mattered to him and it was not recognition.

Polybius was a Greek hostage turned historian, taken to Rome after Macedon's defeat and later attached to the Roman general Scipio. His histories cover the rise of Rome, but the grid he is remembered for was originally a signalling method, meant to be read at a distance rather than kept secret.

Two banks of torches, raised in groups, could spell out a row and column number for each letter, so a message could cross a valley without a runner. Centuries later cryptographers reused the same five by five grid to turn letters into number pairs, which is why a device built for line of sight ended up naming an early cipher.

Paris bridges before this one were crowded with houses and shops built along their length, so a crossing gave no view of the river at all and often blocked it from passersby entirely. Work on a new bridge near the tip of the Ile de la Cite began under Henry III in 1578 and dragged through the wars of religion, finishing under Henry IV, who opened it in 1607.

Built with twelve stone arches and, deliberately, no buildings on its deck, the Pont Neuf gave Parisians their first open sightline down the Seine from a bridge. Its raised pavements, separating pedestrians from cart traffic, were also new to the city. Despite its name, meaning new bridge, it is now the oldest standing bridge across the Seine in Paris.

Telford's aqueduct opened on 26 November 1805 after ten years of building, carrying the Llangollen Canal some 38 metres above the River Dee on eighteen stone piers. The trough itself is cast iron, bolted and flanged rather than riveted, and sealed with a mortar of Welsh flannel soaked in sugar and lead, a detail from the site records rather than folklore.

William Jessop was the engineer of record and Telford the resident engineer who oversaw construction, a division of credit that later biographies often collapse into Telford alone. Boats still cross it today on a towpath cantilevered off one side, with nothing but the iron trough wall between the water and a considerable drop, and it was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009.

Florence had already rebuilt its crossing of the Arno at this narrow point several times since Roman days, each version lost to flood. A catastrophic flood in November 1333 destroyed the previous medieval bridge entirely, and the city commissioned a sturdier replacement, completed by 1345 and credited in tradition to the architect Taddeo Gaddi.

Shops were built directly onto the bridge from the start, originally butchers and tanners whose waste could be tipped straight into the river below, later replaced by goldsmiths after a sixteenth century decree cleaned up the trade. The bridge survived the 1966 Arno flood and, alone among Florence's bridges, was spared deliberate demolition by retreating German forces in 1944.

Afonso Henriques had already been calling himself king for years, since routing his own mother Teresa at the battle of Sao Mamede in 1128 and later claiming a victory over the Moors at Ourique in 1139. What changed in 1143 was recognition: at Zamora, his cousin Alfonso VII of Leon accepted him as king rather than as a rebellious count owing homage.

The Treaty of Zamora did not settle everything, since the papacy withheld formal recognition of Portugal's independence until 1179, decades later. But 1143 is the point at which the county of Portugal, carved out of Leon and Castile during the reconquest, stopped being a contested vassal territory and became a kingdom other rulers had to deal with as one.

The Orloj was installed on the south wall of Prague's Old Town Hall in 1410, built by the clockmaker Mikulas of Kadan with astronomical advice from Jan Sindel, an astronomer at Charles University. Its dial tracks the sun and moon against the zodiac using a geocentric model, so it still shows Earth fixed at the centre with everything else turning around it, exactly as its first audience understood the sky.

A calendar wheel of the months was added later, and a set of moving figures, including a skeletal figure of death that tolls the hour, dates from the nineteenth century rather than 1410. The mechanism itself has been rebuilt and repaired repeatedly after fires and wartime damage, so almost none of the metal turning today is original to the fifteenth century, only the design.

The Kingdom of Hungary had installed a march, a border province, east of the Carpathians to guard against Tatar raids, ruling it through vassal voivodes answerable to the Hungarian crown. Bogdan of Cuhea, a Romanian voivode from neighbouring Maramures who had fallen out with the Hungarian king, crossed the mountains around 1359 and drove out the Hungarian appointed ruler.

Bogdan's revolt turned the Hungarian march into an independent principality, Moldavia, with its own line of rulers and, eventually, its own church hierarchy. Hungary tried repeatedly and failed to reassert control over the following decades. Modern Moldova and much of eastern Romania trace their historical identity to the state Bogdan founded by that act of defection.

In 1477, a Bologna press issued the first printed edition of Ptolemy's Geographia with its maps rendered as engravings rather than hand copied by scribes. Ptolemy had compiled coordinate tables in Alexandria around 150 AD, and for a thousand years each copy of his atlas had drifted slightly from the last through manual reproduction, so no two readers were quite looking at the same world.

Engraving fixed the image once and let a press strike hundreds of identical copies, meaning a scholar in Nuremberg and one in Florence could now argue over exactly the same lines. Later fifteenth century editions began correcting and adding to Ptolemy's outdated Old World geography, but this Bologna printing came first, and it made a shared, checkable map available at a scale no scribe could match.

In 1156 the emperor Frederick Barbarossa issued the Privilegium Minus to settle a dispute over Bavaria, raising the Babenberg march of Austria, previously a lesser border territory, into a duchy in its own right. The charter granted Duke Henry II Jasomirgott special rights, including a rule that let Austria pass to a daughter if no son survived, unusual for the time.

The document survives only as a later, contested copy, which is why historians distinguish it from a hypothetical original, the Privilegium Maius forged two centuries afterward to inflate Habsburg claims further. Genuine or not in every clause, the 1156 charter is the point historians mark as the birth of Austria as a distinct political entity rather than a frontier march.

Utah's ratification on 5 December 1933 gave the Twenty-first Amendment the three-quarters of states it needed, ending the nationwide ban on alcohol that the Eighteenth Amendment had imposed fourteen years earlier. It remains the only constitutional amendment ratified specifically to undo an earlier one.

The new amendment did not simply switch alcohol back on. It handed control to the states, several of which kept their own prohibition laws running for years afterward, Mississippi longest of all, into 1966. It also barred alcohol from being shipped into any state in violation of that state's own laws, a clause still cited in disputes over interstate liquor sales today.

Ptolemy worked in Alexandria, where the old Library still gave a scholar access to centuries of travellers' and surveyors' reports gathered from across the empire and beyond it. His Geographia turned that material into a gazetteer of roughly eight thousand places, each given a latitude and longitude rather than a description in prose.

He also set out mathematical methods for projecting a curved surface onto a flat page, including a conic projection that tried to preserve relative distances. His coordinates were often wrong, sometimes by a wide margin, but the idea of a place fixed by a grid of numbers rather than a story about how to reach it shaped every map that followed.

Before these coins, exchange across northern India ran on weighed metal and barter rather than a struck currency. Around the fifth century BC, the Mahajanapada kingdoms, a cluster of rival states along the Ganges including Magadha and Kosala, began cutting silver into standard weights and stamping each piece with a punch, sometimes several from different issuing authorities on one coin.

The symbols, suns, hills, trees, elephants, are not a script and carry no ruler's name or date, so dating and attributing individual issues still relies on hoards found alongside better-dated material. They mark the start of a monetary economy in South Asia, one that Mauryan and later kingdoms built directly on.

Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard published their scheme, later called BB84 for the year, in 1984, proposing to send a secret key encoded not in numbers on a wire but in the polarisation of individual photons of light. Quantum mechanics guarantees that measuring a photon's polarisation in the wrong way disturbs it, so the two ends of the link could compare a subset of their results afterward to check whether anyone had been listening in.

If an eavesdropper intercepts and measures the photons to read the key, that same disturbance shows up as detectable errors, letting the sender and receiver discard the compromised key and try again. Unlike RSA, whose security rests on a problem believed to be hard, BB84's security rests on a law of physics, and small networks using it have since been built.

Anne became queen in March 1702 on the death of her brother-in-law William III, having already outlived every one of her own seventeen pregnancies, none of which produced a child who survived her. She was the last Stuart to rule and the last British monarch to exercise a personal veto over an act of Parliament, which she used in 1708 to block a Scottish militia bill.

The defining act of her reign was the Union of 1707, which merged the separate Parliaments of England and Scotland into a single Kingdom of Great Britain with one flag and one sovereign. Because she left no heir, the crown passed on her death in 1714 not to a closer Catholic relative but to her German cousin George, Elector of Hanover, under the terms of the earlier Act of Settlement.

The Quran's ban on intoxicants did not arrive as a single flat rule. Earlier verses had only warned that wine carried both benefit and sin, or barred prayer while drunk; a later revelation, traditionally placed around 625, called wine and gambling handiwork of Satan to be avoided outright, and it is this verse that later jurists read as a full prohibition.

The change reordered what was grown and traded across a region where vineyards had supplied Roman and Persian tables for centuries. Grape production shifted toward raisins and syrups, and later Islamic law extended the ban to any fermented drink capable of intoxicating, not wine alone, a scope debated by scholars ever since.

Yigal Amir fired three shots at close range as Yitzhak Rabin walked to his car after a Tel Aviv peace rally on 4 November 1995. Amir was a law student and religious nationalist who had tried at least twice before to get near Rabin, and he later told investigators he acted alone to stop the Oslo Accords from ceding land he believed belonged to Israel by right.

Rabin had signed the accords with Yasser Arafat two years earlier and shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize for it. His killing came amid a campaign of rabbinic rulings and rally placards branding him a traitor and a Nazi, and it hardened rather than paused the argument over the accords, which stalled in the years that followed.

Before 1840, a traveller crossing England could reset their watch several times over, because each town kept its own solar noon: Bristol ran about ten minutes behind London, Exeter further still. That patchwork was tolerable on foot or by coach but dangerous on a railway running to a printed timetable, where two trains could occupy the same track at what each crew thought was a different time.

In November 1840 the Great Western Railway ordered every station along its line to keep London time, set by the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, rather than local time. Other companies followed through the 1840s, long before Parliament made Greenwich Mean Time the legal standard for the whole country in 1880. The railway, not the state, was what actually synchronised Britain's clocks.

On 23 April 1516, Duke Wilhelm IV of Bavaria issued a decree at Ingolstadt fixing what beer sold in his territory could legally contain: barley, hops and water, with yeast's role not yet understood and so left unmentioned. The rule also fixed prices by season, and it was partly a food security measure, since it kept wheat and rye reserved for baking bread rather than competing with brewers for the same grain.

Bavaria's version was not the first such law in German lands, but it outlasted the rest and was extended across a unified Germany in 1906, still cited today as the Reinheitsgebot, the purity law. Brewers elsewhere in Europe used a much wider range of flavourings and preservatives well into the nineteenth century, which is part of why Bavarian beer developed a distinct reputation.

Marian Rejewski was a young mathematician at Poland's Cipher Bureau in 1932, working from intercepted traffic and a commercial Enigma manual, but not from a captured military machine. Germany had wired its army version differently, and nobody outside the factory knew the internal connections of its rotors.

Rejewski used group theory, treating the daily key settings as a mathematical permutation, to deduce that wiring by pure deduction from the patterns in the traffic. French intelligence supplied stolen operating documents that confirmed his reconstruction. The break gave Poland, and later Britain, a working understanding of Enigma years before the war that made codebreaking at Bletchley Park possible.

The Colossus had stood for barely half a century when an earthquake struck Rhodes around 226 BC. Ancient writers say the bronze statue snapped at its weakest point, the knees, and toppled onto land rather than into the harbour it is often shown straddling in later drawings, which have no ancient basis.

Rhodes chose not to rebuild it. An oracle was said to have warned against re-erecting the statue, and the broken bronze pieces lay where they fell for centuries, still impressive enough that Pliny the Elder wrote most people could not span even a single finger with both arms. The remains were eventually sold as scrap metal after the Arab conquest of Rhodes in the seventh century AD.

Matteo Ricci had spent two decades in China learning the language and adapting his Jesuit mission to Ming court conventions before the emperor Wanli asked for a copy of a world map Ricci had shown local officials. Working with the scholars Li Zhizao and Zhong Wentao, Ricci produced Kunyu Wanguo Quantu in 1602, printed as six large woodblock panels meant to be mounted like a folding screen.

The map placed China centrally on the sheet rather than at either edge, a deliberate accommodation of Chinese expectations, and it was the first map in Chinese to include the Americas at all. Only a handful of original copies survive today. It let European geography reach an educated Chinese audience while letting Ricci frame his own presence as one more curiosity worth a place on the map.

Historians had long placed the grave of Richard III somewhere under Leicester, in the ruins of Greyfriars church torn down in the sixteenth century, but the exact spot was gone from memory. In August 2012 a University of Leicester team dug trial trenches in a council car park and, on the first day, found a skeleton with a curved spine and battle wounds to the skull.

DNA taken from two of his living matrilineal descendants matched the remains, confirming in February 2013 that the last Plantagenet king, killed at Bosworth in 1485, had spent over five centuries under a parking bay marked with a painted letter R that nobody had connected to him. He was reburied at Leicester Cathedral in 2015.

Richard was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 3 September 1189, a ceremony marred by a riot against London's Jewish community that broke out after rumours spread that Jews had tried to attend uninvited. Richard had already taken the cross before his father's death and treated the English crown chiefly as a source of money to fund the crusade he intended to lead.

He sold offices, castles and even royal rights to raise funds, reportedly joking that he would have sold London itself if a buyer could be found. Of his ten year reign he spent perhaps six months in England, the rest on crusade, in captivity after being seized on his return journey, or fighting to hold his French territories.

The Venetian state rented a wing of the Palazzo Dandolo near San Moise in 1638 and turned it into a public gaming house, partly to draw players away from the unlicensed rooms already thriving across the city and partly to tax them properly. It ran chiefly during Carnival, when Venice already tolerated a level of disguise unthinkable the rest of the year.

Patrons wore the bauta mask and tricorn hat required at the tables, which let nobles and commoners gamble side by side without anyone officially knowing who was losing what. Games included biribi and basetta, played for stakes high enough that the less wealthy were effectively priced out despite the open door. Mounting complaints about ruin and addiction led the Senate to close it in 1774.

In May 1578, workmen digging along the Via Salaria outside Rome broke through into a network of underground galleries lined with early Christian burials, sealed and largely forgotten since late antiquity. The find drew the antiquarian Antonio Bosio, later called the Columbus of the catacombs, who spent decades crawling through miles of the tunnels by lamplight, mapping passages that had swallowed earlier explorers who lost their way in the dark.

Bosio's survey, published after his death as Roma Sotterranea in 1632, became the foundation of Christian archaeology, cataloguing inscriptions, frescoes and burial niches that offered direct physical evidence of Rome's early church. The rediscovery reframed the catacombs from a rumour into a subject scholars could actually study underground.

By the first century CE, workshops in central Italy were casting oil lamps in two-piece moulds rather than shaping each one by hand, which let a single master pattern be copied thousands of times. The moulds themselves were taken from an existing lamp, so decoration spread from workshop to workshop faster than any individual potter could have carved it.

Many lamps carry a maker's stamp on the base, names like Fortis appearing on finds from Britain to the Black Sea, evidence of production and export on an industrial scale rather than local craft. Those stamps are largely how archaeologists trace trade routes and date the layers they turn up in, since the lamps themselves rarely carry any other record.

Rome's river port at Ostia handled grain, oil and wine unloaded from ships too large to reach the city itself, and cargo regularly went overboard in accidents or storms. The urinatores, whose Latin name simply means divers, worked as an organised trade rather than casual salvagers, diving without any breathing apparatus to recover what had sunk.

Inscriptions record their pay as a fixed share of whatever they brought up, scaled to depth: a diver working in deeper water kept a larger fraction of the goods than one working shallow. That sliding scale, preserved on stone rather than in any literary account, is most of what is known about how the guild actually operated.

Romania's independence was won on a battlefield it did not choose alone. Its army fought alongside Russia against the Ottomans in the war of 1877 to 1878, most visibly at the siege of Plevna in Bulgaria, and that shared campaign was the price of admission when the great powers met afterwards to settle the peace.

The Congress of Berlin in 1878 confirmed Romanian independence but also redrew its map, handing southern Bessarabia back to Russia and giving Romania the Danube delta region of Dobruja in exchange. Full recognition still came with conditions attached: the powers pressed Romania to grant citizenship rights to its Jewish population before treating the new state as fully sovereign.

Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman worked through much of 1977 at MIT trying to build a workable version of the key-exchange idea Diffie and Hellman had published the year before. Shamir and Adleman have said the breakthrough came to Rivest one night after a Passover Seder, and the trio published their scheme, taking their initials as its name, in 1978.

RSA lets anyone encrypt a message using a freely published public key, while only the holder of a matching private key can decrypt it. Breaking it means factoring an enormous number into its two prime components, a problem with no known fast solution. Decades later the algorithm still secures much of the internet, from banking to browser certificates.

Anwar Sadat was killed in Cairo on 6 October 1981, during a military parade marking the anniversary of Egypt's crossing of the Suez Canal in the 1973 war. As a truck towing artillery passed the reviewing stand, Lieutenant Khalid Islambouli forced the driver to stop, then led an armed squad toward Sadat firing rifles and throwing grenades. Sadat reportedly stood to salute them, apparently mistaking the attack for part of the display.

The assault lasted under two minutes and killed Sadat along with several others in the stand. The attackers belonged to Egyptian Islamic Jihad, who regarded Sadat's 1979 peace treaty with Israel as a betrayal deserving death. Islambouli and three co-conspirators were tried and executed the following year; Hosni Mubarak, seated nearby and wounded slightly, succeeded him as president.

The Salisbury clock has no dial and never had one. It exists to ring bells on the hour, striking through a wrought iron frame of weights, gears and a verge escapement built around 1386, work that predates the pendulum by nearly three centuries. It sat first in a bell tower beside the cathedral and was moved inside once that tower was demolished in the eighteenth century.

Restored to running order in 1956 after decades stopped, it is presented as one of the oldest working mechanical clocks anywhere, though a near contemporary at Rouen Cathedral makes the same claim and the two are hard to rank precisely. Both descend from the same monastic need: knowing exactly when to ring the bells that told a town when to pray.

Arthur Samuel wrote his checkers program at IBM in 1959 on a machine, the 701, with barely enough memory to hold the board state, let alone search deep into future moves. His solution was to have the program play thousands of games against itself and against human opponents, adjusting the weights it used to score a position after each game based on whether it had won or lost.

The phrase machine learning appears in the title of Samuel's paper describing the work, one of its earliest uses. By the mid-1960s his program could beat strong amateur players, and IBM used a televised match against Samuel himself, whom it eventually surpassed, to demonstrate that a computer could improve at a task without being reprogrammed by hand.

Tradition holds that Marinus, a stonemason from the Adriatic island of Rab, worked on the rebuilding of Rimini before fleeing Diocletian's persecution of Christians. He climbed nearby Monte Titano and settled there as a hermit rather than as any kind of founder of a state, building a small chapel that drew a community around it.

That settlement is dated to 301 CE and is the basis of San Marino's claim to be the oldest surviving republic in the world, celebrated every year on the third of September as its national day. The tiny state has kept some form of self-government through the fall of Rome, the medieval city-states and Italian unification, never fully absorbed into any of the larger powers around it.

A ship's clock could not survive the pitching of a hull, so European sailors turned to the sandglass, whose falling sand kept time regardless of motion. By the mid-1300s crews were using half-hour glasses to mark the changing of watches, with a ship's boy tasked with turning the glass and striking a bell at each run, work precise enough that a missed turn could throw the whole day's reckoning off.

The same glass, paired with a line knotted at even intervals and trailed behind a moving ship, let sailors count how many knots ran out in a fixed number of turns and so estimate speed. That combination, refined over the following centuries, gave the vocabulary still used for a ship's speed today.

Johann Jacob Schweppe was a Geneva jeweller with a sideline in gasfitting when he refined a process, building on work by Joseph Priestley and others, for saturating water with carbon dioxide under pressure and bottling it so the fizz survived. He began selling it commercially in 1783 and moved the business to London within a decade to reach a bigger market.

Bottled mineral water was sold at first as a health tonic rather than a refreshment, marketed to physicians and sold through chemists. Schweppe's firm went on to supply carbonated water to the royal household and outlasted its founder by more than two centuries, eventually adding the flavoured mixers that carry the name today.

Herodotus was sceptical of his own story. He wrote that Scyllis, a diver from Scione who had recovered wreckage for the Persians after a storm off Mount Pelion, defected to the Greeks before the battle of Artemisium, swimming the whole way underwater, and added that he marvelled if the tale commonly told were true.

What Herodotus does trust is what Scyllis brought with him: a full account of storm damage to the Persian fleet and word that ships were being sent around Euboea to trap the Greeks. Acting on that intelligence, the Greek captains sailed out after midnight and destroyed the detached squadron before it could close the trap.

Sennacherib, the Assyrian king whose army besieged Jerusalem in 701 BCE, was murdered in Nineveh in 681 BCE. Babylonian chronicles and biblical accounts agree only that sons of his killed him, disagreeing on which son and on whether it happened while he was at prayer inside a temple.

The killing set off a succession war won by his son Esarhaddon, who hunted down his rival brothers and later had his own account of the murder carved into official inscriptions, blaming them for it. Assyria's throne passed to Esarhaddon within months, though the killers themselves are never securely named in the surviving record.

Stefan Nemanjic, son of the Serbian state's founder Stefan Nemanja, had ruled as grand prince for years before seeking a crown that would put him on equal footing with neighbouring kings rather than as a lesser regional ruler. In 1217 he obtained one from Pope Honorius III, earning him the byname Stefan the First Crowned.

The choice of a papal, rather than Byzantine, crown was pragmatic: Constantinople was under Latin occupation after the Fourth Crusade and in no position to grant one. His brother Sava, already a monk of standing, secured Serbia's own autocephalous Orthodox church a few years later, so the kingdom's crown and its church came from different, deliberately balanced directions.

Shakey, built at the Stanford Research Institute between 1966 and 1972, got its name from the way its television camera and rangefinder rig visibly wobbled on top of its wheeled base as it moved through a set of rooms built specifically to test it, furnished with wedge- and block-shaped obstacles it had to navigate around.

What made Shakey notable was not the hardware but the software: it could take a general instruction, break it into a sequence of smaller actions, and replan if a planned move turned out to be blocked, rather than simply executing a fixed script. The STRIPS planning system written for it influenced automated planning in artificial intelligence for decades afterward.

Claude Shannon had already founded information theory when, in a 1949 Bell Labs paper on communication theory of secrecy systems, he asked what a cipher would need to be mathematically unbreakable rather than merely hard to break in practice. He defined perfect secrecy as a cipher whose output reveals nothing about the message, even to an attacker with unlimited computing power.

He then proved that only one cipher meets that standard: the one-time pad, a key as long as the message, used once and never reused, with each key never repeated across messages. Every other cipher, however elaborate, leaks some statistical trace of the plaintext. The proof gave cryptographers a fixed benchmark for exactly what security a system could and could not claim.

The game arrived in Persia from India as chaturanga, four battlefield divisions represented by pieces on a board, and Persian players renamed it shatranj and reworked its rules within a few generations. They kept the elephant, chariot, horse and foot soldier but sharpened the endgame, and Persian scribes began writing down finished problems rather than leaving the game to be played and forgotten.

Those written studies, some surviving in Arabic translation, are the earliest chess literature known. When Arab armies took Persia in the seventh century they took shatranj with them, and its vocabulary followed: the shah, or king, is why a losing king is checkmated, from shah mat, the king is helpless.

Until 1967 the second was defined as a fixed fraction of a mean solar day, a unit tied to how fast the Earth happens to spin. That spin turns out to wobble very slightly as tides, earthquakes and the shifting mass of ice sheets nudge it, which made the second an unreliable ruler for physics that needed better precision than the planet could offer.

The 13th General Conference on Weights and Measures redefined the second in 1967 as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation absorbed by a caesium-133 atom transitioning between two energy states, a number chosen to match the old astronomical second as closely as possible. Caesium clocks built to that definition can run for millions of years without gaining or losing a second, and every atomic clock since has used the same standard.

Augustus Siebe, a German instrument maker working in London, sealed his helmet directly to a full waterproofed canvas suit in 1837, closing the open neck the Deane brothers' helmet had left exposed. A valve inside kept the suit from flooding no matter which way the diver turned or bent, unlike the open design it replaced.

Air still came down a hose from a surface pump, but the sealed suit meant a diver could work upside-down or lying flat without water pouring in. Siebe's closed dress became the standard diving suit worldwide, essentially unchanged in principle, and stayed in commercial use for salvage and engineering work into the mid twentieth century.

Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia at midnight on 1 January 1993, an outcome negotiated entirely by parliament rather than settled by referendum or fighting. Polling at the time suggested most citizens on both sides actually opposed dividing the country, but the two dominant political leaders, Vaclav Klaus and Vladimir Meciar, pressed ahead regardless.

Journalists dubbed the split the Velvet Divorce, echoing the largely peaceful Velvet Revolution that had ended communist rule there in 1989. The two new states divided federal assets, including the army and diplomatic missions, through negotiation rather than conflict, and both went on to join the European Union together in 2004.

Diving bells before John Smeaton's version carried only the air trapped inside them when they were lowered, which fouled with carbon dioxide within minutes and forced divers back to the surface. Working on harbour repairs in the 1780s, Smeaton fitted a cast-iron bell with a hose connected to a force pump worked by assistants on a boat above.

The pump pushed a continuous supply of fresh air down into the bell, letting stale air escape and letting divers stay under far longer than any earlier design allowed. Smeaton used it on his own harbour works at Ramsgate, and the fed-air principle behind it carried through into the diving suits and caissons of the following century.

When cholera tore through Soho in the summer of 1854, killing roughly 600 people in the surrounding streets within about ten days, the accepted theory was that a poisonous miasma in the air caused it. John Snow, a local doctor already sceptical of that idea, instead walked the neighbourhood interviewing families of the dead and marking each death as a black bar on a street map.

The bars piled up thickest around a single public water pump on Broad Street. Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump handle, and although the outbreak was already subsiding by then, his map and his interviews built a case for waterborne transmission that later investigation confirmed: a leaking cesspit near the pump had contaminated its well. The map is now treated as a founding document of epidemiology.

A severe earthquake struck Sparta around 464 BC. Ancient sources, principally Plutarch and Diodorus, describe buildings collapsing across the city and heavy loss of life, though no reliable death count survives from a state that kept few written records of itself by design.

The disaster's real consequence was political. Sparta depended on enslaved Messenian helots to work its land, and the chaos of the quake gave them an opening: a revolt broke out that dragged on for roughly a decade, forcing Sparta to call on allied cities, including Athens, for help putting it down.

The scytale was a wooden rod, and a message written by winding a leather strip around it in a spiral came out as scattered letters once unwound flat. A commander in the field carried a rod of matching diameter; wind the strip around it the same way and the letters lined back up into readable text.

Plutarch describes Spartan generals receiving orders this way, including the recall of the admiral Lysander near the end of the Peloponnesian War around 404 BC. Modern cryptographers class it as a transposition cipher rather than genuine encryption, since the letters themselves are never changed, only their order, which a captured strip alone could not easily undo without the matching rod.

John Bellingham, a Liverpool merchant ruined by a failed business venture in Russia, blamed the government for refusing to compensate him and had petitioned Parliament repeatedly without result. On 11 May 1812 he waited in the lobby outside the House of Commons and shot Spencer Perceval once through the chest with a pistol he had commissioned specifically for the act.

Perceval died within minutes, the only British prime minister ever assassinated, and Bellingham made no attempt to escape, telling bystanders he had been denied justice. He was tried within a week, convicted, and hanged outside Newgate Prison on 18 May 1812, a trial widely criticised even at the time for its speed.

Spermaceti is the waxy oil found in a cavity in a sperm whale's head, and by the 1750s Rhode Island merchants had worked out how to press and refine it into a hard, pale candle that burned steadier and brighter than tallow and without tallow's smell or smoke. Newport and Providence families, the Rivera and Brown among them, built refineries around the trade.

The candles became a colonial luxury good and an export in their own right, sold from Newport to London at a fixed price the makers colluded to hold. The unit they burned in became a rough standard of brightness, later formalised as the candlepower still used to describe light output, well after gas and electric lighting had made whale oil obsolete.

Lawrence Sperry was twenty years old when he flew the first test of his father's gyroscope-driven stabiliser on a Curtiss flying boat at Hammondsport, New York, late in 1912. Two spinning gyroscopes sensed pitch and roll and moved the elevators and ailerons to correct them, keeping the aircraft level without a hand on the controls.

The idea proved itself two years later in Paris, where Sperry flew low over the Seine, stood up with both hands raised while his mechanic walked out onto the wing, and let the machine hold itself steady. The stunt won the Concours de la Securite prize of fifty thousand francs and made the case for automatic flight that the 1912 device had first demonstrated.

Prince Thutmose is said to have fallen asleep beside the half-buried Sphinx and dreamed that the monument, if freed of sand, would make him king. The pink granite Dream Stele he later placed between its paws records the promise. He did become king, as Thutmose IV, around 1400 BCE, and credited the clearing of the drifts to that dream.

The Sphinx was already thirteen centuries old at that point, carved from the Giza plateau's bedrock in the age of Khafre, and had already needed rescuing from the desert once before Thutmose's crews dug it out again. Wind-blown sand kept refilling the hollow around it for millennia, and later clearings, including a twentieth-century one, faced the same problem.

Suleiman the Magnificent ordered the bridge in 1557 to replace an older wooden suspension crossing over the Neretva that locals thought was unsafe. Its architect, Mimar Hayruddin, had trained under Sinan, the great architect of Ottoman Istanbul, and construction of the single stone arch took nine years, finishing in 1566.

The arch spans about 27 metres and rises 4 metres wide, high enough above the Neretva gorge that local divers jumping from it became a Mostar tradition of its own. The bridge stood for 427 years until Croat forces shelled it apart in November 1993 during the Bosnian war; it was rebuilt using much of the original stone recovered from the riverbed and reopened in 2004.

A 1957 paper by Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle, known ever since by the authors' initials as B2FH, ran to more than a hundred pages and worked through how stars fuse hydrogen and helium into carbon, oxygen, iron and almost every heavier element on the periodic table, using nuclear physics rather than assumption to fix the ratios.

The paper mattered because it broke with George Gamow's picture of the early universe forging all the elements in one hot burst; B2FH showed most of them are made continuously, inside stars, over billions of years. Elements heavier than iron require a dying star's supernova to force them into existence, meaning the calcium in bone and the iron in blood were both cooked in stars that exploded long before the Sun formed.

Stephen was born Vajk, a prince of the Magyar chieftain Geza, and took the Christian name Stephen at his baptism. On his coronation, traditionally dated to Christmas Day 1000 or 1 January 1001, he wore a crown said to have been sent by Pope Sylvester II, a gift that let him claim kingship rather than mere overlordship.

The crown became Hungary's central relic of legitimacy, though the surviving Holy Crown of Hungary is now dated by scholars to well after Stephen's lifetime. What is not in doubt is the change he forced through: the loose Magyar tribal confederation became a single Christian kingdom with dioceses, counties and a royal law code.

Strasbourg Cathedral installed an astronomical clock in the 1350s built to display far more than the hour: a calendar, the positions of the sun and moon, and moving figures that acted out the passage of time for a largely illiterate congregation. Its most talked about feature was a gilded copper cock mounted near the top.

At noon each day the mechanical bird spread its wings, parted its beak and let out a crow, driven by bellows and gears hidden inside the casing, likely the oldest automaton of its kind still known from medieval Europe. The clock as a whole was replaced twice in later centuries, but the surviving cock from this original machine is now kept and displayed separately as one of the few working parts of it left.

Su Song built his water driven clock tower at the Song capital, Kaifeng, work beginning around 1088 and the finished structure ready by 1092. Water filled buckets on a wheel at a steady rate, tripping an early escapement that let the wheel advance in fixed steps rather than spinning freely, the same basic problem later solved differently by mechanical clocks in Europe.

A chain drive Su Song called the celestial ladder linked the wheel to 133 wooden figures that emerged through doors to strike bells, beat drums and hold up placards marking the hour. His illustrated treatise on the mechanism survived, but the tower itself did not: Jurchen invaders dismantled it in 1126 and carried the parts north as war spoils.

Basil Brown was a self-taught archaeologist working for the landowner Edith Pretty when he opened the largest of the mounds at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk in 1939. The ship's timbers had rotted away entirely, but their impression survived in the sand as a ghost outline nearly ninety feet long, rivets still in place where the planks had been.

Inside a collapsed burial chamber at the ship's centre lay a hoard nobody had expected from Anglo-Saxon England: a helmet, gold buckles and shoulder clasps set with garnet, silver bowls, and coins that helped date the burial to around 620. No body was ever found, dissolved by the acidic soil, but the wealth argued for a king, most likely Raedwald of East Anglia.

Thucydides describes the obstacle rather than naming the divers who beat it. Syracuse, besieged by an Athenian fleet during the Sicilian Expedition, drove rows of stakes into the harbour mouth, some visible and some cut off below the waterline where a ship's hull would strike them unseen.

Athenian sailors dived on the submerged stakes and sawed through them, though Thucydides notes some were bolted with iron and harder to shift than the wooden ones. Clearing them mattered less than the campaign around it: the siege of Syracuse ended in 413 BC in the destruction of the Athenian fleet and army, a defeat from which Athens never fully recovered.

In 622 BCE, workmen repairing the Jerusalem Temple under King Josiah found a scroll of law that the high priest Hilkiah brought before the king. Hearing it read aloud, Josiah tore his clothes in grief at warnings his kingdom had apparently ignored, then ordered a purge of local shrines and a national Passover.

Many biblical scholars think the scroll was some version of Deuteronomy, either genuinely rediscovered or freshly written to justify reforms already under way, since its language and concerns match that book closely. Either way, the find gave Josiah's changes the weight of an old, forgotten law rather than a new royal decree.

Before the wheel-thrown terracotta lamp, households burned oil in open bowls or pinched-clay saucers, both wasteful and prone to spilling. From around 700 BCE, potters across the Mediterranean mass-produced a cheap, closed lamp with a spout to hold the wick, letting a household burn olive oil with far less waste and less fire risk.

These lamps are so common on excavation sites that archaeologists use their shape and decoration to date the layers around them almost like coins. Production stayed a household craft rather than an industry, made and sold in local workshops, until moulded lamps in Hellenistic and Roman times let makers copy one popular design by the thousand.

Marc Brunel's tunnel between Rotherhithe and Wapping had almost failed twice, flooded by the Thames in 1827 and again in 1828, an accident that nearly killed his young son and assistant engineer Isambard. The project then stalled for seven years for lack of money until a government loan let it resume. Marc's invention, a heavy iron shield that let miners dig a small face at a time while supported, was what made a river crossing survivable.

It opened to the public on 25 March 1843 as a pedestrian tunnel, not the road link originally planned, and became a tourist attraction and a market lined with stalls rather than the trade route investors had hoped for. It was later fitted with rails and is still in use, carrying London Underground trains through the same brick bore.

Marie Tharp was barred from the research ships that gathered sonar soundings of the Atlantic seabed in the 1950s because women were not allowed aboard, so she worked from the data her colleague Bruce Heezen brought back, plotting depth profiles by hand onto paper at Columbia's Lamont Geological Observatory through 1957.

When she drew the profiles side by side, a long valley kept appearing down the centre of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Heezen initially dismissed it as impossible, calling it girl talk, but the rift matched newly plotted earthquake locations exactly. It became key evidence for continental drift and seafloor spreading, ideas most geologists still rejected when Tharp first drew the line.

Ancient writers mentioned a port called Thonis where Helen and Paris supposedly landed en route to Troy, but no ruins matched it on any modern map, because the city was not on the coast anymore. Franck Goddio's team, surveying Abu Qir Bay near Alexandria with sonar and magnetometers, found it under several metres of silt and seawater in 2000.

Thonis and the Greek trading colony of Heracleion turned out to be the same place, known by two names to two peoples who had assumed they were separate. Slabs naming Pharaoh Nectanebo I, a giant temple to Amun-Gereb, and sunken ships still holding their cargo let archaeologists date the city's slow sinking, likely from earthquakes and rising sea levels, to around the eighth century AD.

Titan lost contact with its surface ship less than two hours into its descent on 18 June 2023, carrying tourists paying around 250,000 dollars each to view the Titanic wreck two and a half miles down. A multinational search located debris four days later on the seafloor, close to the wreck itself.

The five people killed were OceanGate's chief executive Stockton Rush, British explorer Hamish Harding, veteran Titanic diver Paul-Henri Nargeolet, and the father and son Shahzada and Suleman Dawood. Investigators traced the loss to the carbon fibre hull, a material never before used at that depth in a crewed submersible, which had shown signs of delamination on earlier dives.

Tomislav became duke of Croatia around 910 and spent the next years absorbing neighbouring Croatian duchies and holding off both Hungarian raids from the north and Bulgarian pressure from the east. By the mid 920s he controlled enough territory, and enough recognition from Rome, that later tradition credits him with taking the title of king.

No contemporary document records the coronation itself, and even the year, usually given as 924 or 925, rests on later chronicles rather than a surviving charter. What is firmer is that a synod under papal legates addressed him as king around that time, which is the documentary basis for treating him as the first king of a united Croatian realm.

Trajan needed a fixed crossing to move legions into Dacia rather than relying on boats, and his architect Apollodorus of Damascus built one on twenty masonry piers sunk into the Danube's bed, each pair carrying a timber arch about 38 metres across. The whole structure ran roughly 1,135 metres, the first bridge over the lower Danube.

It was finished in 105 CE after a build of about two years and was the longest arch bridge in the world, by both span and total length, for over a thousand years. Trajan's successor Hadrian removed its wooden superstructure and Aurelian later abandoned the province entirely, leaving only the stone piers that still stand in the riverbed.

Johannes Trithemius was a Benedictine abbot in Sponheim who spent his life defending himself against a rumour that his earlier book on angels was black magic. Polygraphiae, printed in 1518, two years after his death, was his answer: cryptography dressed as harmless devotional Latin, dedicated to Emperor Maximilian rather than hidden from him.

Its table assigns each letter of the alphabet its own column of code words, so enciphering a message and reading off the columns in order produces a string of Latin that looks like a prayer. A message hidden this way could pass as pious nonsense to anyone who intercepted it, which is why historians credit Trithemius as the first printed author on the subject rather than merely an early one.

Sandor Just and Franjo Hanaman filed their Hungarian patent for a tungsten filament bulb in December 1904, working in Budapest. Tungsten's appeal was its melting point, far higher than the carbon threads Edison had used, which meant the filament could run hotter and give off more light for the same electricity without burning through as quickly.

Making a usable filament was the hard part: tungsten's brittleness had to be worked around by extruding a paste of tungsten powder through a fine die and then baking off the binder in hydrogen. Commercial tungsten bulbs reached the market within a few years and displaced carbon-filament lamps almost entirely, the basic technology that lit homes until LED bulbs took over a century later.

Drawn under Ramesses IV around 1150 BCE, the Turin Papyrus shows the gold and stone quarries of Wadi Hammamat in Egypt's Eastern Desert: coloured bands marking granite, black and pink rock, dry stream beds, and the huts and wells along the route. It is the oldest geological map known to survive from anywhere.

The papyrus was made for a practical purpose, guiding an expedition sent to haul stone for a royal statue, not for record's sake. It survives only in fragments, reassembled from pieces held in Turin, and its accuracy has let modern geologists match its rock colours to the wadi's actual strata.

The first bombe, named Victory, began running at Bletchley Park on 18 March 1940, built to Turing's design and refined with Gordon Welchman's addition of the diagonal board, which cut the search space dramatically. It was an electromechanical machine of spinning drums, each standing in for one of Enigma's rotors, testing thousands of possible settings against a guessed fragment of plaintext.

A working bombe did not read a message directly; it ruled out settings until only a handful remained plausible, which codebreakers then tested by hand. More than two hundred bombes were eventually built and run day and night by Wrens, recovering the German military's daily Enigma keys often within hours of the traffic being intercepted.

Alan Turing was twenty-three when his paper On Computable Numbers appeared in 1936, written to answer David Hilbert's question of whether a definite procedure could decide any mathematical statement's provability. Turing imagined a simple machine reading and writing symbols on an endless tape according to fixed rules, a device with no physical form that could still stand for any calculation a person could carry out by hand.

He proved that no such general procedure exists, because some questions about the machine's own behaviour, such as whether it will ever stop running, cannot be settled in advance for every case. The machine itself, an abstraction meant only to answer a question in logic, became the working blueprint for what a stored-program computer would later actually do.

Juanelo Turriano was Philip II's court clockmaker, credited with an elaborate water-lifting works at Toledo alongside his automata. According to the story attached to this one, Philip's son Don Carlos was badly injured and the king vowed a miracle in return for his recovery, then commissioned a moving likeness of the Franciscan friar Diego de Alcala once the boy survived.

The friar, about 38 centimetres tall and driven by a wound spring turning iron cams beneath its robe, walks a small square path, beats its chest with one arm, raises a cross and rosary with the other, turns its head and moves its lips as if praying. It survives at the Smithsonian, still able to run through its routine after more than four centuries, one of the oldest complex automata still working.

David Bushnell's Turtle was a one-man oak shell shaped like two turtle backs joined together, ballasted with water and driven by hand-cranked propellers. On the night of 6 September 1776, Sergeant Ezra Lee piloted it into New York harbour toward HMS Eagle, the anchored British flagship, meaning to screw a powder charge into her hull and swim clear before it exploded.

Lee reached the hull but could not drive the screw through it, most likely because he had struck an iron strap reinforcing the ship's bottom, and after repeated tries he gave up and turned for shore as daylight came on. The charge detonated harmlessly in the harbour. It was the first submarine attack on a warship in recorded history, even though it failed.

Ptolemy's planetary system worked well enough to predict positions, but it leaned on the equant, a point not at the centre of a circle from which motion was defined as uniform. Astronomers at the Maragha observatory in Persia treated that as a flaw in principle, not just a technical fix, and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi set out to remove it entirely.

His solution, described in 1261, combined two circles: a small one rolling inside a larger one twice its size, so that a point on the small circle traces a straight line back and forth. Two such rotating circles could reproduce the oscillating motion the equant faked without one. Copernicus used the same device three centuries later, unattributed, in his own planetary models.

On 11 November 1572, Tycho Brahe noticed a point of light in Cassiopeia brighter than Venus, in a spot where no star belonged. Aristotelian cosmology held that everything beyond the Moon was fixed and unchanging, so a genuinely new light among the stars, rather than something nearer like a comet, was not supposed to be possible.

Tycho measured its position against neighbouring stars for months and found no parallax shift at all, proving it lay among the fixed stars rather than in the sublunar sphere where change was permitted. He published De Nova Stella in 1573, and what he had actually seen, unknown to him, was a supernova, the explosive death of a star, now catalogued as SN 1572 and still visible as a faint remnant to modern telescopes.

Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, voted for independence on 24 August 1991, days after a failed coup against Mikhail Gorbachev in Moscow exposed how weak the Soviet centre had become. The vote came suddenly, catching even some of its own deputies by surprise at how far events had moved.

The declaration still needed public backing to carry weight, and on 1 December 1991 a referendum returned over 90 percent in favour, with majorities in every region including Crimea and the mostly Russian-speaking east. A week later, leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed an agreement effectively dissolving the Soviet Union, which formally ceased to exist before the year was out.

George Devol patented a programmable mechanical arm in the 1950s and, with the engineer Joseph Engelberger, built it into a commercial machine called Unimate. General Motors installed the first one in 1961 at its die-casting plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, where the job was pulling red-hot metal castings from a die-casting machine and stacking them, a task too hot and repetitive for a human worker on every shift.

Unimate followed a sequence recorded onto a magnetic drum rather than sensing its surroundings, and it could not adapt if a part shifted out of place.
