Even so, it proved an arm could work unsupervised on a factory line without breaking down, and Engelberger's company Unimation went on to sell the design across the American auto industry through the following decade.

By early 1862 the Union's ability to pay for the Civil War was outrunning its gold reserves, and borrowing alone could not cover the bills. Congress responded with the Legal Tender Act, authorising the Treasury to print paper dollars, printed with green ink on the back, that were not redeemable in gold or silver on demand.

The bills, quickly nicknamed greenbacks, were declared legal tender for nearly all debts, forcing creditors to accept paper where they had previously expected coin. Their value floated against gold for years and dipped sharply when the war went badly for the Union, but the government never withdrew them, and the greenback established the precedent, still in force, that United States currency need not be backed by precious metal at all.

The first leap second was inserted at midnight on 30 June 1972, the day Coordinated Universal Time switched from a stretched second to a fixed one matching the atomic caesium standard. Earth's spin is not perfectly steady, and clocks kept by atoms had begun drifting ahead of clocks kept by the planet's own rotation.

Rather than let the gap grow, the international timekeeping bodies agreed to freeze an extra second onto UTC whenever the difference approached a full second, keeping civil time within 0.9 seconds of solar time. More than two dozen leap seconds have followed since 1972, each announced months in advance and each capable of quietly breaking software that assumes a minute always has sixty of them.

Douzhen Xinfa, a text on smallpox from 1549, is the earliest surviving Chinese record of deliberately giving someone a mild case of the disease to prevent a severe one. Physicians dried scabs from smallpox pustules, ground them to powder and blew them up a healthy person's nose through a tube, aiming for an infection light enough to survive and leave lasting immunity.

The method was refined further around Huangshan in Anhui during the later Ming dynasty and stayed a regional, largely folk practice for generations rather than a state programme. It travelled outward slowly, reaching Russia, Central Asia and Japan over the following two centuries, well before variolation reached England and was adapted there into Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine.

The warship Vasa capsized and sank in Stockholm harbour on its maiden voyage in 1628, taking dozens of bronze cannons to the bottom with it. Bronze was valuable enough that Sweden hired Hans Albrekt von Treileben, a former army officer, and the German salvager Andreas Peckell to get the guns back rather than write them off.

Their tool was a diving bell, an open-bottomed chamber lowered on a rope that trapped a pocket of air a diver could breathe from while working blind in cold water with hooks and tongs. Over 1664 and 1665 they recovered 53 of the ship's 64 cannons, each weighing well over a tonne, a remarkable haul given the equipment. The hull itself, and its remaining guns, stayed on the harbour floor for another three centuries.

Jacques de Vaucanson unveiled his mechanical duck in Paris in 1739 alongside a flute player and a tambourine player, both genuine musical automata built to prove machines could reproduce living motion rather than just imitate a clock's tick. The duck was the crowd-pleaser: gilded copper, over four hundred moving parts in each wing, and a bill that took grain and appeared to pass it through a digestive tract.

The digestion was a trick. Grain vanished into a hidden reservoir while a separate stored paste, dyed to look like waste, came out the other end, a fact confirmed once later owners took the duck apart. Vaucanson never denied the deception outright, and the phrase Voltaire is said to have used, comparing him to a rival inventor, kept the duck famous long after it stopped working and was eventually lost.

Gilbert Vernam, an engineer at AT&T, worked out his cipher in 1917 and received the patent, number 1,310,719, in 1919. It combined each letter of a teleprinter message with a letter from a key tape using an electrical add operation, so the output looked like noise unless the receiver held an identical tape.

Vernam had used a repeating key, which left a weakness a skilled cryptanalyst could exploit. Joseph Mauborgne of the Army Signal Corps saw that a truly random key, used only once and never repeated, closed that gap entirely. The combination, later called the one-time pad, is the only cipher ever proven mathematically unbreakable.

Victoria was eighteen and had been woken before dawn on 20 June 1837 to be told her uncle William IV had died overnight, making her queen. She had grown up sheltered under her mother's strict Kensington System, largely kept apart from the court, and her first act as monarch was reportedly to insist on seeing the Privy Council alone rather than with her mother present.

She was crowned the following year, on 28 June 1838, and went on to reign for 63 years, then the longest of any British monarch, a record only surpassed by Elizabeth II in 2015. The stretch of industrial and imperial expansion that filled those decades came to carry her name as the Victorian era.

The Geheime Kabinettskanzlei ran out of Vienna's main post office, where clerks worked before dawn. Sealed letters passing through were opened over steam, read, copied in a fair hand, resealed with forged wax impressions matched to the original seals, and sent on their way before the morning post left, so neither sender nor recipient ever knew.

Similar bureaux existed in Paris, Berlin and other capitals, but Vienna's black chamber ran longest and was studied as the model. Its decrypts went straight to the emperor and his ministers, giving Habsburg diplomacy a standing advantage over ambassadors who assumed their dispatches were private. The office survived into the nineteenth century before its methods became public knowledge.

Radiocarbon dating of the vellum places the Voynich manuscript's creation around 1420, well before the antiquarian Wilfrid Voynich who gave it his name bought it from a Jesuit college in 1912. Its roughly 240 surviving pages are filled with an unbroken invented script, alongside drawings of unidentifiable plants, nude women bathing in green liquid through tubes, and star charts that match no known constellation system.

Codebreakers who cracked German and Japanese military ciphers in the twentieth century have tried it and failed, as have statistical linguists comparing its letter patterns to real languages. The leading theories range between an unknown natural language, a deliberate hoax, and a genuine but unrecoverable cipher, and none has produced a translation that other specialists accept.

Albrecht von Wallenstein commanded the Habsburg armies through much of the Thirty Years' War, and his private diplomacy with Protestant enemies convinced Emperor Ferdinand II that he was negotiating a peace on his own account. Ferdinand stripped him of command in January 1634 and had a secret court convict him of treason without his knowledge.

On 25 February 1634 a group of Irish and Scottish officers in his own army, acting under Ferdinand's approval, killed Wallenstein and several companions at Eger. Colonel Walter Butler led the assassins; the garrison's commandant, John Gordon, and his deputy, Walter Leslie, had already been marked as willing. Ferdinand later rewarded them with property confiscated from Wallenstein's family.

At Smithfield on 15 June 1381, the fourteen-year-old Richard II met the rebel leader Wat Tyler to negotiate an end to the Peasants' Revolt. Accounts differ on who moved first, but the Lord Mayor of London, William Walworth, drew a dagger and cut Tyler down in front of his own followers, who had gathered outside the city walls after burning the Savoy Palace and freeing prisoners days earlier.

Richard rode toward the stunned crowd and shouted that he himself would be their leader, buying time while armed men mustered. Tyler's head was displayed on London Bridge. The king's promises of freedom and lower rents were withdrawn within weeks, and Parliament reaffirmed serfdom, but the revolt had already forced the abandonment of the poll tax that provoked it.

Steam engines before 1788 needed a person watching the throttle constantly, because their speed climbed or sagged with every change in load. James Watt adapted a governor already used on windmills: two weighted arms spinning on a vertical shaft driven by the engine itself, flying outward as speed rose and dropping back as it fell.

The arms' movement was linked directly to the throttle valve, so a rising engine speed choked its own steam supply and a falling one opened it again, with no attendant needed to intervene. The device became a standard textbook example of feedback control long before that phrase existed, and its self-correcting logic underpins automatic regulators well beyond steam engines.

Robert Whitehead built his torpedo from a rough sketch handed to him by an Austrian naval officer, Giovanni Luppis, whose own version was a small unmanned boat steered by ropes from shore. Whitehead, an English engineer working in Fiume, threw out the boat and built a cigar-shaped hull driven by compressed air, tested on the Adriatic from 1866.

The device everyone wanted to copy was inside a sealed compartment called the balance chamber. A pendulum swinging fore and aft was linked to a spring-loaded valve reading water pressure, and together they drove the horizontal rudders that held the torpedo level at a set depth. Whitehead kept the mechanism secret for years, and navies paid to license it rather than reverse it.

William the Silent had led the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule for over a decade and survived at least one earlier attempt on his life. On 10 July 1584, Balthasar Gerard, posing as a Protestant refugee seeking a letter of introduction, shot him at close range on the stairs of his house in Delft.

Philip II of Spain had put a price on William's head, and Gerard had come specifically to collect it; he was captured, tortured and executed within days. William's death did not break the revolt he had led. His son Maurice took up the fight, and the northern provinces went on to secure their independence as the Dutch Republic.

Benny Binion invited a handful of the country's best-known professional gamblers to his Horseshoe Casino in downtown Las Vegas in May 1970, not for a structured tournament but for a run of cash games played over several days among a small, invited group, an event he was reviving after buying the rights to a similar Reno gathering.

There was no prize pool and no bracket. At the end, the assembled players simply voted on who among them had played the best, and Johnny Moss was named champion, receiving a silver cup rather than any cash. The following year's event switched to a freeze-out format that eliminated players by chip count, the structure the World Series of Poker has used ever since.

Herodotus says the first attempt failed: a storm wrecked an earlier set of cables, and Xerxes had the strait itself whipped and branded for its insolence before ordering a second crossing built. Persian engineers anchored hundreds of ships bow to stern across the Hellespont, near modern Canakkale, and laid planking and packed earth over cables of flax and papyrus to carry the roadway.

Two parallel bridges carried the army over separately, one for troops and pack animals, the other kept clear so nothing held up the march. Herodotus put the crossing at seven days and nights without rest, an army large enough that ancient counts of a million or more are now treated as wild exaggeration rather than record.

The story comes from the Daoist text Liezi, written centuries after the supposed event: the artificer Yan Shi presented King Mu of Zhou, who is placed in the tenth century BCE, with a life-size figure of wood and leather that walked, tilted its head, and sang when its chin was touched.

The demonstration turned dangerous when the figure winked at the king's concubines, and Mu, taking it for a living rival, ordered Yan Shi executed on the spot. The craftsman tore the figure apart to show the king its jointed wood and painted leather held no life at all, saving himself and leaving one of the earliest robot stories on record.

Alexandre Yersin arrived in Hong Kong in 1894 to a colonial epidemic and a rival already working the same wards: the Japanese bacteriologist Kitasato Shibasaburo, backed by better facilities and getting there first. Yersin, with a borrowed hut for a laboratory, took his samples from the buboes of the dead rather than the blood Kitasato favoured, and found a consistent rod-shaped bacterium the Japanese team had missed.

Yersin's bacterium was confirmed as the cause of bubonic plague and later named Yersinia pestis in his honour. The identification did not immediately explain how the disease spread; the role of fleas carried on rats was worked out separately over the following decade, but pinning the bacterium down gave researchers something to test treatments and diagnoses against.

The Yu Ji Tu, carved into stone in 1136, mapped China's rivers, coastline and mountain ranges over a regular square grid, each cell representing a fixed distance on the ground. That grid system for measuring scale on a map traced back centuries in Chinese cartography, to methods credited to the third century official Pei Xiu.

What struck later observers is how closely the coastline and river courses on the stone match a modern map, achieved without instruments for measuring longitude. The carving was meant for administrators governing the Song empire, a practical tool for a state that needed to know its own rivers and borders in exact proportion, not a decorative chart.

Zhang Heng held the post of Chief Astronomer at the Han court, a job that combined astronomy with calendar-keeping and omen reading for the emperor. His surviving writing on the subject, the Ling Xian, describes the moon as a ball that receives its light from the sun rather than glowing on its own.

From that he reasoned that a lunar eclipse happens when the moon passes through the cone of shadow the Earth casts opposite the sun. He also built a water-driven armillary sphere to model the sky's motion, work that put him a step ahead of most contemporaries anywhere in explaining eclipses as geometry rather than omen.

The Zodiac Killer sent the FBI a 340 character cryptogram in 1969, made of odd symbols substituting for letters, and unlike his earlier 408 character cipher it resisted every codebreaker for more than fifty years, including the FBI's own cryptanalysis unit and the NSA.

In December 2020, David Oranchak, a software developer, Sam Blake, an Australian mathematician, and Jarl Van Eycke, a Belgian programmer, cracked it using custom pattern-matching software the trio had built between them. The message contained no name and no confession, mostly a taunting claim about an afterlife, and the killer's identity remains unknown.

Fritz Zwicky measured the velocities of galaxies in the Coma cluster in 1933 and found them moving so fast that the cluster's visible stars could not possibly hold it together gravitationally; it should have flown apart long before. He proposed that some unseen form of matter, which he called dunkle Materie, made up most of the cluster's mass and kept it bound.

The idea was largely set aside for decades, partly because Zwicky's manner made him easy to dismiss and partly because the evidence was indirect. It was vindicated only in the 1970s, when Vera Rubin's studies of galaxy rotation found the same gap between visible mass and the gravity actually observed, turning Zwicky's inference into one of astronomy's central open problems.
